High Probability Risk Control for
Online Policy Learning

Yihong Guo    Drew Prinster    Suchi Saria    Anqi Liu Affiliation: Johns Hopkins University Email: {yguo80,aprinst1,ssaria1,aliu.cs}@jhu.edu
Abstract

We study risk control for online policy learning, where an agent adaptively collects data and aims to learn a new policy whose risk stays below a tolerance threshold at every round with high probability. Such policy updates and data collection induce feedback covariate shift (FCS): observed data depend on history through evolving policies and the data-collection process. FCS brings two substantive problems for risk control: 1) efficient risk evaluation for each candidate policy and 2) valid policy selection with high-probability risk control. To address these, we propose a permutation-based weighted risk evaluator with weights efficiently approximated by the Sinkhorn algorithm and select policies whose estimated risk upper confidence bounds (UCB) fall below the target threshold, with the UCB obtained through a proposed Gaussian bootstrap method. Theoretically, we prove that our risk evaluator has a no-larger variance upper bound than that of the standard importance-weighted evaluator. Our policy control method also yields an asymptotically valid simultaneous risk bound and provides asymptotic high-probability risk control for the selected policy. Empirically, we evaluate our method on the online contextual bandit problem, safe question answering benchmark, and Medical Claim Filtering tasks. Our method maintains the target risk level, achieves lower risk than baseline methods, has lower variance in risk estimation, and achieves reliable policy selection with high-probability risk control. Further ablation studies support our theoretical claims.

1 Introduction

Machine learning (ML) / artificial intelligence (AI) systems can be applied to sequential decision-making in high-stakes settings such as healthcare [1] and autonomous driving [2], but deployed models should adhere to constraints such as safety, fairness, and the law. In other words, responsible model deployment often requires controlling the risk of such constraint violations.

We study risk control for online policy learning with adaptive data collection and the policy learning process. Across sequential rounds of deployment, the goal is to repeatedly select a learned policy (i.e., a distribution over actions) to deploy whose risk is below a prescribed threshold. At each round, the agent updates a policy using historical data, calibrates its risk with tuning parameters, deploys the calibrated policy, and then incorporates the newly collected data into the next update.

While Prinster et al. [3] developed a framework for this policy control problem (building on ideas from conformal risk control [4]) with guarantees that hold in expectation over the risk of constraint violations, here we focus on a stronger desideratum of risk control with an (asymptotic) high-probability guarantee: the risk of the selected deployment policy is below a tolerance threshold with high probability. This introduces at least two key challenges for high-probability risk control: (1) efficient risk evaluation for each candidate policy and (2) policy selection while maintaining valid high-probability guarantees. That is, at each round, one requires not only a valid estimate of each candidate policy’s risk, but also a valid procedure for choosing a policy to deploy without selection bias corrupting the decision [3]. Our paper focuses on the two aspects of high-probability risk control.

Efficient risk evaluation is difficult in online policy learning because adaptive data collection induces feedback covariate shift [5, 6]: the policy and the observed data distribution change over time as a function of the history during the online learning process. Under FCS, standard importance-weighted approaches may be invalid because they do not account for sequential dependencies; moreover, such estimators can suffer from high variance when policies diverge and encounter extreme values, which is common when the policy changes quickly. To address this, we extend the permutation-based weighted method for CP in Prinster et al. [6] to risk evaluation under FCS and theoretically show that the proposed evaluator has no greater variance upper bound than the standard importance-weighted evaluator. However, such permutation marginal weights are intractable (factorial complexity). Therefore, we formulate permutation-based weight computation as a variational solution to a constrained optimization problem that can be solved efficiently using the Sinkhorn algorithm [7].

A second challenge is high-probability risk control. While existing works such as conformal policy control (CPC) [3] or CRC [4] only guarantee that the expected risk is below the threshold, we propose a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap for policy control on top of the risk estimator to achieve an asymptotic high-probability guarantee, which provides an empirical risk upper bound and does not require i.i.d. data. Specifically, our method estimates the worst-case inflation of the risk estimate over all λ\lambda, yielding a simultaneous upper bound over the candidate set. Selecting policies with UCBs below the threshold ensures that all selected policies satisfy the risk threshold with asymptotic high probability.

2 Preliminaries and Related Work

2.1 Online Policy Learning and Risk Control

At each round tt, a learner observes a context Xt∈𝒳X_{t}\in\mathcal{X}, selects an action At∈𝒜A_{t}\in\mathcal{A}, and receives a reward Rt∈ℝR_{t}\in\mathbb{R} and a bounded loss Lt∈[0,B]L_{t}\in[0,B]. Let Zt=(Xt,At,Rt,Lt)Z_{t}=(X_{t},A_{t},R_{t},L_{t}) and Z1:t=(Z1,…,Zt)Z_{1:t}=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{t}) denote the observation and ordered history. Using this history, the learner updates a base policy πθt+1\pi_{\theta}^{t+1}. Rather than deploying the policy directly, we select from a candidate family {πθ,λt+1:λ∈Λ}\{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}:\lambda\in\Lambda\}, where λ\lambda adjusts the policy’s action distribution, such as temperature, and thereby its reward–risk trade-off. The goal is to select λ^t+1\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1} such that ℓt+1(λ^t+1):=𝔼πθ,λ^t+1t+1[Lt+1(Xt+1,At+1)∣Z1:t,Xt+1]≤α,\ell_{t+1}(\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1}):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta,\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1}}^{t+1}}\left[L_{t+1}(X_{t+1},A_{t+1})\mid Z_{1:t},X_{t+1}\right]\leq\alpha, where α\alpha is the risk tolerance. We assume that the candidate set Λ\Lambda is finite. We also assume access to a known fallback policy πsafe\pi_{\mathrm{safe}} whose deployment risk is at most α\alpha. A marginal guarantee controls expected risk below the tolerance threshold at every round: 𝔼⁡[ℓt+1​(λ^t+1)]≤α\mathbb{E}[\ell_{t+1}(\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1})]\leq\alpha. The high-probability objective instead controls the probability of exceeding the tolerance every round: ℙ⁡(ℓt+1​(λ^t+1)>α)≤δ,\mathbb{P}(\ell_{t+1}(\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1})>\alpha)\leq\delta, where δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) is the allowed failure probability.

2.2 Feedback Covariate Shift and Conformal Risk/Policy Control

Feedback Covariate Shift. Online policy updates create a challenge for risk control at every round: The policy deployed at each round depends on past observations, while also determining the distribution of future collected data. This adaptive data-collection process induces feedback covariate shift and produces dependent, generally non-exchangeable observations. It differs from non-adaptive covariate shift or non-adaptive policy shift, where the sampling policies are independent of the observed data, and there is no such sequential dependency among data observations. Building on weighted conformal prediction under fixed covariate shift [8], subsequent work studies single-round [5] and multi-round FCS [9, 6]. Sample-wise importance ratios account for differences between behavior and target policies, but do not explicitly account for such sequential data dependency and feedback covariate shift. Permutation-based weighting accounts for the joint sampling mechanism, including its dependence on the observation history, but direct computation becomes intractable as the history grows [6].

Conformal Risk Control. Conformal risk control (CRC) [4] extends conformal prediction [10] to control the expectation of any bounded loss function Li​(λ)L_{i}(\lambda) that is monotonically parameterized by some tuning parameter, λ\lambda. For example, CRC recovers conformal prediction for the miscoverage loss Li(λ):=𝟏{Yi∉C^λ(Xi)}L_{i}(\lambda):=\mathbf{1}\{Y_{i}\not\in\hat{C}_{\lambda}(X_{i})\}, where λ\lambda controls the size of a prediction set C^λ​(Xi)\hat{C}_{\lambda}(X_{i}) to reduce the risk of not including YiY_{i}. Or, λ\lambda could be a classification threshold that monotonically reduces the false negative rate. Related approaches, including Bates et al. [11] and learn-then-test (LTT) [12], provide high-probability risk control for non-monotonic losses under i.i.d. data. However, these guarantees do not directly apply to the adaptive policy learning setting with feedback covariate shift.

Conformal Policy Control (CPC). CPC [3] is most related to our work. Rather than assuming a loss Li​(λ)L_{i}(\lambda) that can be directly tuned by a parameter λ\lambda, CPC accommodates losses LiL_{i} that admit no tuning parameter at all, by instead having λ\lambda index a family of policies, {πθ,λt+1:λ∈Λ}\{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}:\lambda\in\Lambda\}. For example, the constraint violation indicator loss Li:=𝟏{Ai∉𝒮}L_{i}:=\mathbf{1}\{A_{i}\not\in\mathcal{S}\}, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a set of safe or allowable actions, is not a function of any tuning parameter λ\lambda; CPC controls the expectation of such losses by instead tuning the action distribution that the expectation is taken over. Its conservative selection rule, λ^CPC=inf{λ0∈Λ:supλ∈Λ,λ≥λ0[∑i=1tpi​(λ)​Li+pmax​(λ)​B]≤α},\widehat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{CPC}}=\inf\{\lambda_{0}\in\Lambda:\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\in\Lambda,\lambda\geq\lambda_{0}\end{subarray}}[\sum_{i=1}^{t}p_{i}(\lambda)L_{i}+p_{\max}(\lambda)B]\leq\alpha\}, handles non-monotonicity in the policy search, where pi​(λ)p_{i}(\lambda) are normalized permutation weights that account for the FCS (to be introduced in Section 3.1) and pmax​(λ)p_{\max}(\lambda) is the worst-case test-point weight used in the correction. With exact permutation weights, CPC guarantees risk control in expectation: 𝔼⁡[ℓt+1​(λ^t+1)]≤α\mathbb{E}[\ell_{t+1}(\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1})]\leq\alpha.

Addressing Limitations of CPC: Efficient Weight Estimation and High-Probability Risk Control. CPC, however, still has at least two limitations, which our paper aims to address: First, CPC’s guarantee only applies for exact permutation weights, and Prinster et al. [3] do not theoretically characterize any relation of their practical estimates (based on mixture weights) to the exact permutation weights. Our first contribution addresses this gap by formulating permutation-weight computation as a constrained optimization problem that can be efficiently estimated via the Sinkhorn algorithm, and shows that the resulting risk evaluator has no greater variance upper bound than the standard importance-weight method. Second, the marginal expectation form of CPC’s guarantee does not necessarily guarantee risk control for a particular calibration set, as in the desideratum, due to potentially high variance. To address this limitation, we focus on obtaining an asymptotic high probability guarantee, which says: lim supt→∞ℙ⁡(ℓt+1​(λ^t+1)>α)≤δ\limsup_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\!(\ell_{t+1}(\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1})>\alpha)\leq\delta. Note that we mainly focus on the adaptive policy learning setting as in CPC, but our risk control component can apply to non-adaptive covariate shift settings.

Additional related work is provided in Appendix A.

3 Method

In this section, we introduce our main algorithm. We first introduce a permutation-based weighted risk estimator to evaluate next-round risk that accounts for FCS, extending the permutation-based weighted method for CP in [6] to risk estimation. To reduce the computational cost of computing permutation weights exactly, we introduce an efficient estimation method with a constrained optimization problem. With this efficient risk evaluator, our method, Risk Control for Policy Learning in Expectation (RCL-E), can achieve risk control in expectation under a monotonic risk function. Then, we introduce our policy selection method through a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap method to obtain an asymptotic high-probability risk control guarantee, namely Risk Control for Policy Learning with High Probability (RCL-HP). We summarize our algorithm in Algorithm B.

3.1 Efficient Evaluation of Candidate Policy Risks

3.1.1 Preliminaries for Permutation-Based Risk Estimation under Feedback Covariate Shift

Adapting the key idea from Prinster et al. [6] to our setting, we account for FCS by analyzing the risk conditionally on the bag (or multiset) of calibration and test data, Ez:={Z1:t+1}E_{z}:=\{Z_{1:t+1}\}, and drawing permutations from the bag with probabilities given by the sequence of historical policies, πθ,λ1:t+1:=(πθ,λ11,…,πθ,λt+1t+1)\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1:t+1}:=(\pi_{\theta,\lambda_{1}}^{1},...,\pi_{\theta,\lambda_{t+1}}^{t+1}), letting λ=λt+1\lambda=\lambda_{t+1}. Importantly, note that the bag EzE_{z} conveys the information that the random variable Lt+1L_{t+1} will take a value from the observed values {l1:t+1}\{l_{1:t+1}\}, but we do not know which value (see Prinster et al. [6] for details). The bag-conditional risk is then

ℓ(λ):=𝔼πθ,λ1:t+1[Lt+1∣Ez]=∑i=1t+1li⋅ℙπθ,λ1:t+1(Lt+1=li∣Ez),\displaystyle\textstyle\ell(\lambda):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1:t+1}}\big[L_{t+1}\mid E_{z}\big]=\sum_{i=1}^{t+1}l_{i}\cdot\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1:t+1}}\big(L_{t+1}=l_{i}\mid E_{z}\big), (3.1)

where ℙπθ,λ1:t+1(Lt+1=li∣Ez)\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1:t+1}}\big(L_{t+1}=l_{i}\mid E_{z}\big) can be interpreted as the probability of drawing a sequence of values from EzE_{z} such that the test loss, Lt+1L_{t+1}, is observed to be the value lil_{i}. As described in Prinster et al. [6] (which explains analysis from Tibshirani et al. [8]), these probability weights can be expanded via the law of total probability over permutations, σ:[t+1]→[t+1]\sigma:[t+1]\rightarrow[t+1], as

pi(λ):=ℙπθ,λ1:t+1(Lt+1=li∣Ez)=∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=iπ(zσ⁡(1),…,zσ⁡(t+1))∑σπ⁡(zσ⁡(1),…,zσ⁡(t+1)),p_{i}(\lambda):=\mathbb{P}_{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1:t+1}}\big(L_{t+1}=l_{i}\mid E_{z}\big)=\frac{\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(t+1)=i}\pi(z_{\sigma(1)},...,z_{\sigma(t+1)})}{\sum_{\sigma}\pi(z_{\sigma(1)},...,z_{\sigma(t+1)})}, (3.2)

where π\pi denotes the joint distribution induced by the policies πθ,λ1:t+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1:t+1} for more concise notation.

Together, Eq. (3.1) and Eq. (3.2) thus clarify how permutation-based weights offer a natural and valid, though computationally intimidating, target for risk evaluation under the candidate policy, πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}. These weights account for the adaptive data collection process and stand in contrast to standard sample-wise importance weights. Moreover, in our setting we assume that the context distribution is i.i.d., so the context distribution cancels out in Eq. (3.2) (see Appendix C.1) and the marginal permutation weights pi​(λ)p_{i}(\lambda) are a function of the historical context-dependent policies, {πθ,λi​(a∣x)}\{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{i}(a\mid x)\}.

As described in Prinster et al. [3], however, a key difference from the CP setting in Prinster et al. [6] is that here we wish to estimate the risk of the policy πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1} before sampling the next action, At+1A_{t+1}. Accordingly, we simulate a hypothetical test sample Zt+1Z_{t+1} and conservatively assume it receives the worst-case loss, Lt+1=BL_{t+1}=B. That is, we conservatively estimate the expected risk as

ℓ^​(λ):=∑i=1tli⋅pi​(λ)+B⋅pt+1​(λ).\textstyle\widehat{\ell}(\lambda):=\sum_{i=1}^{t}l_{i}\cdot p_{i}(\lambda)+B\cdot p_{t+1}(\lambda). (3.3)

3.1.2 Efficiently Approximating the Permutation Weight

The exact permutation marginal (Eq. (3.2)) easily becomes intractable as the number of rounds grows. Prinster et al. [6] proposed a surrogate approximation that considers only the permutation of the most recent position assignment rather than the full permutation assignment. Instead, we approximate the permutation marginals via entropy-relaxed variational inference over doubly stochastic matrices, whose rows and columns each sum to 1. This leads to a tractable doubly-stochastic assignment matrix computed via Sinkhorn iterations [7, 13, 14].

To efficiently obtain the permutation marginal pi​(λ)p_{i}(\lambda), we use an entropy-regularized marginal approximation. We denote the policy matrix J∈ℝ+(t+1)×(t+1)J\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{(t+1)\times(t+1)}, where Jk,i:=πk​(Ai∣Xi)J_{k,i}:=\pi_{k}(A_{i}\mid X_{i}). Each element Jk,iJ_{k,i} represents the density that policy kk places on the data point ii, irrespective of the other data points. We further let Q⋆Q^{\star} be the permutation marginal: each entry Qk,i⋆Q^{\star}_{k,i} represents the probability that sample ii occupies position kk in a permutation drawn from the bag, EzE_{z}. The following Theorem states that the permutation marginal weight Q⋆Q^{\star} is a weight matrix close to the original policy matrix JJ, subject to the permutation constraint that each data point is mapped uniquely to one position.

Theorem 3.1 (Sinkhorn approximation of permutation marginal weights).

We approximate the permutation marginal weights by the entropy-relaxed surrogate:

Q⋆=argminQ∈ℬt+1KL(Q∥J),ℬt+1={Q∈ℝ+(t+1)×(t+1):Q𝟏=𝟏,Q⊤𝟏=𝟏}.\displaystyle Q^{\star}=\arg\min_{Q\in\mathcal{B}_{t+1}}\mathrm{KL}(Q\|J),\qquad\mathcal{B}_{t+1}=\left\{Q\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{(t+1)\times(t+1)}:Q\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},\;Q^{\top}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}\right\}. (3.4)

Then Q⋆Q^{\star}’s last row provides an approximation to the permutation marginal weights:

pi(λ)≈Qt+1,i⋆,i=1,…,t+1.\displaystyle\textstyle p_{i}(\lambda)\approx Q^{\star}_{t+1,i},\qquad i=1,\dots,t+1.
Remark 3.2.

Theorem 3.1 provides a tractable surrogate for the exact permutation marginal. Instead of summing over exponentially many feasible assignments, we relax the exact assignment to an entropic assignment marginal and solve a convex KL projection problem. The constraint set ℬt+1\mathcal{B}_{t+1} preserves the global one-to-one structure of a permutation, where Qi,jQ_{i,j} represents the probability of data point jj being assigned at position ii. Because each data point is assigned to one position and each position is assigned one data point, the row and column sums of QQ are 1. The optimizer can be computed by matrix scaling, and its last row Qt+1,i⋆Q^{\star}_{t+1,i} serves as the approximate permutation weight for evaluating the target policy at the final round. The derivations are in Appendix C.4. The optimization problem can be solved efficiently via Sinkhorn/IPFP [7] through iterative matrix scaling, as described in Appendix C.5 and Algorithm 2.

Sources of Approximation. The matrix Q⋆Q^{\star} approximates the permutation marginal because the optimization problem is an entropy-relaxed surrogate of the exact marginal inference objective. The exact objective has an intractable entropy term: the entropy of the permutation. We replace the intractable entropy of the full permutation distribution by an entrywise entropy relaxation: H(σ)≈H(Q)=−∑i​jQi​jlogQi​jH(\sigma)\approx H(Q)=-\sum_{ij}Q_{ij}\log Q_{ij}. In Appendix G.6.1, we empirically evaluate the approximation error of the Sinkhorn approximation and show it is small. We also provide a theoretical analysis of how the error affects later risk estimation and guarantees in Appendix G.6.2.

Interpretation of the Permutation-based Estimator. We provide how we can calculate the exact permutation marginal in Appendix C.1 following Prinster et al. [6]. We now further interpret the permutation-based risk evaluator in the following propositions.

Proposition 3.3 (Reduction to SNIPS under standard covariate shift).

Suppose all historical data are collected by a fixed behavior policy πb\pi_{b}, and the next-round risk is evaluated under the target policy πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}. Then the exact permutation marginal weight under the fixed policy sequence reduces to the Self-Normalized Importance Sampling (SNIPS) weight: pi​(λ)=πθ,λt+1​(Ai∣Xi)/πb​(Ai∣Xi)∑j=1t+1πθ,λt+1​(Aj∣Xj)/πb​(Aj∣Xj)p_{i}(\lambda)=\frac{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})/\pi_{b}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{j}\mid X_{j})/\pi_{b}(A_{j}\mid X_{j})}.

Proposition 3.4 (Permutation weight as a global importance weight).

Under the fixed policy sequence πθ,λ1,…,πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1},\ldots,\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}, the exact permutation marginal weight can be written as pi​(λ)=πθ,λt+1​(Ai∣Xi)​Ci,t+1∑k=1t+1πθ,λk​(Ai∣Xi)​Ci,kp_{i}(\lambda)=\frac{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})\,C_{i,t+1}}{\sum_{k=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{k}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})\,C_{i,k}}, where Ci,k:=∑σ:σ⁡(k)=i∏h=1,h≠kt+1πθ,λh(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h))C_{i,k}:=\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(k)=i}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}h=1,h\neq k\end{subarray}}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}) denotes the total contribution of all feasible assignments in which sample ii occupies position kk.

Remark 3.5.

Proposition 3.3 shows that the permutation weights reduce to the SNIPS in the covariate shift setting, and Proposition 3.4 shows their connection to importance sampling under a fixed policy sequence. Classic sample-wise importance weights are local, depending only on the ratio between the candidate policy and the behavior policy for the realized sample. In contrast, permutation weights are global, normalized weights: each weight depends not only on the corresponding policy likelihood but also on the entire observed data bag and all feasible assignments. This is what allows the estimator to account for the sequential dependence and potentially provide a smoother importance weight.

3.2 Bootstrap Policy Control for Asymptotic High-Probability Guarantees

Risk Control in Expectation under Monotonicity. With our efficient risk evaluator, we propose a CPC/CRC-style risk control when the risk is monotonic. For the selected λ^=inf{λ:ℓ^​(λ)≤α}\hat{\lambda}=\inf\{\lambda:\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)\leq\alpha\}, our method RCL-E has: 𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(λ^)]≤α\mathbb{E}[\ell(\hat{\lambda})]\leq\alpha, where the risk is controlled in expectation. Under monotonicity, RCL-E can be viewed as CPC [3] with our efficient Sinkhorn-based weight estimation.

High Probability Risk Control. However, when the risk function is non-monotonic, or we want to achieve high-probability risk control, selecting λ\lambda through λ^=inf{λ:ℓ^​(λ)≤α}\hat{\lambda}=\inf\{\lambda:\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)\leq\alpha\} does not provide the desired guarantee. We now introduce our policy selection method for high-probability risk control, namely RCL-HP. To guarantee high-probability risk control after this policy selection step, it is not enough to ensure high-probability risk control of each fixed candidate separately. Instead, we need to ensure that no unsafe candidate enters the estimated feasible set: ℙ(∃λ∈Λ^feas:ℓ(λ)>α)≤δ\mathbb{P}(\exists\lambda\in\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}}:\ell(\lambda)>\alpha)\leq\delta.

We construct a simultaneous uncertainty correction over the entire candidate set Λ\Lambda. The correction uses the largest risk underestimation error, T=supλ∈Λ{ℓ⁡(λ)−ℓ^​(λ)}T=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\{\ell(\lambda)-\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)\}. Let q1−δq_{1-\delta} be the (1−δ)(1-\delta)-quantile of T. Then ℓ⁡(λ)+q1−δ\ell(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta} is a simultaneous upper confidence bound over Λ\Lambda. Define the feasible set as: Λ^feas={λ∈Λ:ℓ^​(λ)+q1−δ≤α}\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}}=\{\lambda\in\Lambda:\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta}\leq\alpha\}.

Theorem 3.6 (High probability risk control with true q1−δq_{1-\delta}).

With q1−δq_{1-\delta} as the true value of the (1−δ)(1-\delta)-quantile of TT, and Λ^feas={λ∈Λ:ℓ^​(λ)+q1−δ≤α}\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}}=\{\lambda\in\Lambda:\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta}\leq\alpha\}, we have ℙ(∃λ∈Λ^feas:ℓ(λ)>α)≤δ\mathbb{P}(\exists\lambda\in\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}}:\ell(\lambda)>\alpha)\leq\delta.

Remark 3.7.

Theorem 3.6 shows that if the true quantile q1−δq_{1-\delta} were available, then the policy selection rule achieves high-probability risk control. The q1−δq_{1-\delta} acts as a uniform safety margin that accounts for the worst underestimation error over the entire candidate family, rather than the error of a single fixed candidate. This lets us control the policy and select a policy from the candidate set regardless of the non-monotonic loss. Consequently, the policy selected from Λ^feas\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}} satisfies the risk constraint with high probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. The proof is given in Appendix D. This result assumes access to the true (1−δ)(1-\delta)-quantile of the maximal underestimation error. In practice, this quantile is unknown. We approximate its distribution using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap, establish bootstrap consistency in Theorem 4.5, and obtain the asymptotic guarantee in Corollary 4.7.

Gaussian Multiplier Bootstrap to Approximate q1−δq_{1-\delta}. A direct resampling bootstrap is inappropriate because the data are collected adaptively rather than i.i.d., and resampling raw observations would distort the sequential data-collection mechanism. Instead, we apply a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap [15]. Let ℓ^​(λ)\widehat{\ell}(\lambda) denote the base risk estimator, and let ϕ^i​(λ)\widehat{\phi}_{i}(\lambda) denote the contribution of sample ZiZ_{i} to the linearized estimation error at parameter λ\lambda: ϕ^i​(λ)=pi​(λ)​(Li−ℓ^​(λ))\textstyle\widehat{\phi}_{i}(\lambda)=p_{i}(\lambda)\bigl(L_{i}-\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)\bigr). Given independent multipliers ζi​∼i.i.d.​N​(0,1)\zeta_{i}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}N(0,1), we define the bootstrap process

G^t+1∗​(λ)=∑i=1t+1ζi​ϕ^i​(λ).\displaystyle\textstyle\widehat{G}_{t+1}^{*}(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{t+1}\zeta_{i}\,\widehat{\phi}_{i}(\lambda).

For each bootstrap draw, we compute the maximal fluctuation T∗=supλ∈ΛG^t+1∗​(λ),T^{*}=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\widehat{G}_{t+1}^{*}(\lambda), and repeat this procedure to obtain an empirical approximation to the distribution of the maximal risk-estimation error. Then, using this distribution, we can obtain the 1−δ1-\delta quantile of TT and select a policy. However, since we approximate it with high probability, we can only obtain an asymptotic high-probability risk control with bootstrap consistency rather than a finite-sample guarantee.

4 Theoretical Analysis

In Theorem 4.3, we show that our method achieves a variance upper bound no larger than that of the standard importance weight estimator. In Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 4.7, we show the asymptotic high-probability risk control of our policy selection method.

Proposition 4.1 (Weight upper bounds).

Let n=t+1n=t+1, m=|𝒜|<∞m=|\mathcal{A}|<\infty, and Mϵ=[1−(m−1)​ϵ]/ϵM_{\epsilon}=[1-(m-1)\epsilon]/\epsilon. Assume all historical policies πθ,λii\pi_{\theta,\lambda_{i}}^{i} and the candidate πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1} satisfy π⁡(a∣x)≥ϵ\pi(a\mid x)\geq\epsilon for all (x,a)(x,a), with 0<ϵ≤1/m0<\epsilon\leq 1/m. For the positive, normalized permutation weights pp, assume Δp:=log⁡(maxi⁡pi/mini⁡pi)≤ΔJ:=log⁡(maxk,i⁡Jk,i/mink,i⁡Jk,i)\Delta_{p}:=\log(\max_{i}p_{i}/\min_{i}p_{i})\leq\Delta_{J}:=\log(\max_{k,i}J_{k,i}/\min_{k,i}J_{k,i}), i,e., the log range of the weight matrix does not increase after the permutation. For the importance weight, set ωi=πθ,λt+1​(Ai∣Xi)/πθ,λii​(Ai∣Xi)\omega_{i}=\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})/\pi_{\theta,\lambda_{i}}^{i}(A_{i}\mid X_{i}) for i≤ti\leq t, and ωn=1\omega_{n}=1 for the candidate policy. Then

maxipi≤MϵMϵ+n−1=:aperm,maxiωin≤Mϵn=:aIPS.\displaystyle\max_{i}p_{i}\leq\frac{M_{\epsilon}}{M_{\epsilon}+n-1}=:a_{\mathrm{perm}},\qquad\max_{i}\frac{\omega_{i}}{n}\leq\frac{M_{\epsilon}}{n}=:a_{\mathrm{IPS}}. (4.1)

Hence aperm≤aIPSa_{\mathrm{perm}}\leq a_{\mathrm{IPS}}.

Remark 4.2.

A smaller log-range Δp≤ΔJ\Delta_{p}\leq\Delta_{J} indicates more uniform weight. Under Δp≤ΔJ\Delta_{p}\leq\Delta_{J}, Proposition 4.1 gives a no-larger upper bound for permutation weight than for IPS, namely aperm≤aIPSa_{\mathrm{perm}}\leq a_{\mathrm{IPS}}. Under Proposition 4.1, for the bounded losses, put L~i=Li\widetilde{L}_{i}=L_{i} for i≤ti\leq t and L~n=B\widetilde{L}_{n}=B. Theorem 4.5 (Bootstrap validity in high probability risk control).

Under Assumption F.1, consider a fixed finite candidate family Λt+1\Lambda_{t+1} and define

Tt+1=supλ∈Λt+1{ℓt+1​(λ)−ℓ^t+1​(λ)}.\displaystyle\textstyle T_{t+1}=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{t+1}}\bigl\{\ell_{t+1}(\lambda)-\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda)\bigr\}.

For each λj∈Λt+1\lambda_{j}\in\Lambda_{t+1}, define

ϕ^i​(λj)=pi​(λj)​{L~i−ℓ^t+1​(λj)},G^t+1∗​(λj)=∑i=1t+1ζi​ϕ^i​(λj),\displaystyle\textstyle\widehat{\phi}_{i}(\lambda_{j})=p_{i}(\lambda_{j})\bigl\{\widetilde{L}_{i}-\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})\bigr\},\qquad\widehat{G}_{t+1}^{*}(\lambda_{j})=\sum_{i=1}^{t+1}\zeta_{i}\widehat{\phi}_{i}(\lambda_{j}),

where L~i=Li\widetilde{L}_{i}=L_{i} for i≤ti\leq t, L~t+1=B\widetilde{L}_{t+1}=B for the test point, and ζi​∼i.i.d.​N​(0,1)\zeta_{i}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}N(0,1) are independent of the data and shared across candidates. Define

Tt+1∗=supλ∈Λt+1G^t+1∗​(λ).\displaystyle\textstyle T_{t+1}^{*}=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{t+1}}\widehat{G}_{t+1}^{*}(\lambda).

For fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), let q1−δ,t+1∗q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*} be the (1−δ)(1-\delta)-quantile of Tt+1∗T_{t+1}^{*} given 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. Then, as t→∞t\to\infty,

supu∈ℝ|ℙ⁡(Tt+1≤u)−ℙ⁡(Tt+1∗≤u∣𝒟t)|→𝑝0.\displaystyle\textstyle\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\mathbb{P}(T_{t+1}\leq u)-\mathbb{P}(T_{t+1}^{*}\leq u\mid\mathcal{D}_{t})\right|\xrightarrow{p}0.

Moreover,

ℙ⁡(ℓt+1​(λ)≤ℓ^t+1​(λ)+q1−δ,t+1∗,for all ​λ∈Λt+1)⟶1−δ.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\ell_{t+1}(\lambda)\leq\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*},\ \text{for all }\lambda\in\Lambda_{t+1}\right)\longrightarrow 1-\delta.
Remark 4.6.

Theorem 4.5 justifies that the bootstrap approximation of the error can asymptotically represent the true underestimation error of the risk estimate. So we can obtain a valid q1−δq_{1-\delta} quantile for the error, leading to the asymptotically high-probability guarantee in the following Corollary 4.7. The assumption includes a fixed finite family of candidate policies, uniformly positive action probabilities, and adaptive logging policies satisfying the finite-dimensional affine structure and stabilization conditions in Assumption F.1.

Proof Sketch: We first derive a first-order linear expansion of the estimation error under Assumption F.1 in terms of the policy sequence. Then, we show that for each candidate policy, the ground-truth estimation error and the bootstrap-estimated error converge asymptotically to the same Gaussian distribution. Then, the ground-truth and the estimated maximum error among all candidate policies follow the same distribution, and the bootstrap quantile is a valid approximation of the true error. The complete proof is given in Appendix F. Appendix G.6.4 provides empirical and theoretical diagnostics and verification of the Lemma and Assumptions.

Corollary 4.7 (Asymptotic High Probability Risk Control).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.5, define the feasible set Λ^t+1,feas:={λ∈Λt+1:ℓ^t+1​(λ)+q1−δ,t+1∗≤α}.\widehat{\Lambda}_{t+1,\mathrm{feas}}:=\{\lambda\in\Lambda_{t+1}:\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*}\leq\alpha\}. If the selected parameter λ^t+1\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1} is restricted to Λ^t+1,feas\widehat{\Lambda}_{t+1,\mathrm{feas}} or fallback to default safe policy πsafe\pi_{\text{safe}}, then

lim supt→∞ℙ⁡(ℓt+1​(λ^t+1)>α)≤δ.\displaystyle\textstyle\limsup_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\!(\ell_{t+1}(\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1})>\alpha)\leq\delta.

Moreover, lim inft→∞ℙ⁡(ℓt+1​(λ)≤α​ for all ​λ∈Λ^t+1,feas)≥1−δ\liminf_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\!(\ell_{t+1}(\lambda)\leq\alpha\text{ for all }\lambda\in\widehat{\Lambda}_{t+1,\mathrm{feas}})\geq 1-\delta.

Remark 4.8.

Corollary 4.7 converts the simultaneous bootstrap UCB into a high-probability guarantee: after screening by the corrected risk estimate, any chosen λ^t+1\widehat{\lambda}_{t+1} is asymptotically safe up to error probability δ\delta. The final statement corresponds to controlling the family-wise error of selecting at least one candidate that violates any risk constraint.

5 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the empirical risk control performance on different online learning applications in Section 5.1 and 5.2. We show the benefit of our permutation-based weighted risk evaluator in Section 5.3. We compare with high-probability control methods and show that it effectively accounts for feedback covariate shift while maintaining high-probability risk control without being overly conservative in Appendix G.5. We also provide additional results on permutation weight approximation error and bootstrap validity diagnostics in Appendices G.6.1, G.6.4, respectively. The code is available at: https://github.com/guoyihonggyh/High-Probability-Risk-Control

5.1 Risk Control in Expectation and High Probability Risk Control

We briefly introduce the baselines, datasets, tasks, risk definition, as well as the policy and update rules. Appendix G.3 details the baselines, and Appendix G.1 details the task settings.

Baselines: Online CRC (O-CRC) [4] extends CRC under the distribution shift setting to online learning and uses importance weighting to account for the policy shift. RollingRC [16] utilizes the adaptive conformal inference (ACI) [17] to adapt to the distribution shift. Conformal Policy Control (CPC) [3] uses a similar permutation-weighting idea as ours but provides a control method for a non-monotonic risk function. Note that CPC in our implementation exactly matches RCL-E in the monotonic risk-function setting and uses its proposed control method in the non-monotonic risk-function setting. We also compare against the permutation weight estimation method originally proposed in [6]. Details are in Appendix G.3. We do not compare against Learn-then-Test (LTT) here because it requires i.i.d. data, but we discuss and compare it with our RCL-HP in a later section.

Datasets and Tasks: We conduct experiments on two online contextual bandit tasks, breast cancer diagnosis [18] and stock investment [19], and one LLM safe question answering task with SafetyBench [20]. For breast cancer diagnosis, the policy controls the false negative rate of breast cancer diagnosis. For stock investment, the policy controls the probability of selecting the worst action below the threshold. For SafetyBench Question Answering, the policy controls the error rate by refusing to answer questions. The breast cancer diagnosis is a monotonic risk setting; the remaining two tasks are non-monotonic risk settings. We summarize how the λ\lambda affects the policy, which risk is controlled, and whether the risk function is monotonic in Table 1.

Data Collection and Policy Update: We initialize with m0m_{0} offline samples split into training and calibration sets. Each round collects mm new samples, splits them equally between the two sets, and updates the policy using training data until the data budget is reached. We set (m0,m)=(50,20)(m_{0},m)=(50,20) for Breast Cancer Diagnosis and (300,50)(300,50) for Stock Investment. For safe question answering, we use SFT checkpoints from the base model as a fixed policy sequence to induce larger policy changes and potentially stronger covariate shift. Figure 4 shows checkpoint validation accuracy. Calibration starts with m0=512m_{0}=512 and collects m=128m=128 samples per round, using data from the preceding step without training data or policy updates. This non-adaptive sequence simulates online policy optimization but does not constitute feedback covariate shift. We adopt it to evaluate risk estimation and high-probability risk control under potentially larger shifts than standard online learning.

Remark 5.1.

Our work is primarily motivated by feedback covariate shift induced by online policy updates, with deployment risk controlled by adjusting the policy’s action distribution. Our experiments also consider non-adaptive covariate shift and risk-control settings. In the non-adaptive setting, the policy sequence is independent of the observed data. Our SafetyBench experiment follows this setting, with no feedback-driven policy updates, and such a setting can create a larger distribution shift than standard online policy learning with feedback covariate shift in this dataset. MedicalQA, discussed in Section 5.2, illustrates the risk-control framework described in CRC [4]. Table 2 summarizes the control objectives and distribution-shift settings across our experiments. Appendix G.2 further clarifies the distinctions between risk control and policy control, and between feedback covariate shift and non-adaptive covariate shift.

Results: Figure 1 shows the main results. We first evaluate our method, RCL-E risk control in expectation, on a monotonic risk function with breast cancer. We do not report the CPC in breast cancer as it is the same as RCL-E. We show that, compared with the baseline that controls risk in expectation, our method maintains risk below the threshold from the start with a small dataset, while the baselines require more data to meet the constraint. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our permutation-based risk estimator. We then evaluate our method, RCL-HP high-probability risk control, on three datasets. Across the three datasets, RCL-HP achieves the lowest risk. In terms of risk satisfaction, our method empirically achieves high-probability risk control.

5.2 Evaluation of High-Probability Risk Control in Factual Medical QA

Datasets: We evaluate the RCL-HP on the MedLFQA dataset Jeong et al. [21]. The dataset of Cherian et al. [22] contains GPT-3.5-Turbo responses, atomic subclaims extracted via GPT-4o, and factuality annotations obtained by checking each subclaim against reference answers. Given a confidence score p⁡(Ci​j|Xi)p(C_{ij}|X_{i}) for each sub-claim, we filter claims below a threshold λ\lambda and measure the false discovery rate (FDR), the fraction of retained claims that are false, as our risk. The reward is recall, the fraction of total true claims retained. We calibrate the GPT-4o confidence threshold, without sequential data collection or policy updates, to evaluate Gaussian-bootstrap high-probability risk control in the standard fixed-distribution setting. Risk is non-monotonic in λ\lambda. Experimental settings are summarized in Tables 1 and 2.

Baselines: In this setting, we mainly compare the control method in [3] rather than the risk estimator, since there is no policy update and no distribution shift. Generalized conformal policy control (gCRC) extends conformal policy control to the one-step risk control setting without policy updates, using the same policy selection method as CPC. Monotonic-risk CRC addresses non-monotonic risk by monotonizing the risk for each data point in λ\lambda and then applying standard conformal risk control to the resulting monotonic risk function. Learn-then-Test (LTT) [12] treats each candidate policy as a hypothesis and tests whether its risk is below the target threshold. Details of the baselines and the task setting are in Appendix G.1.4.

Results: Figure 2 shows FDR and recall across risk levels, α\alpha. RCL-HP controls FDR at or below the target level across all α\alpha values while also achieving a high-probability guarantee that FDR stays below the target level. gCRC is less conservative but does not empirically provide a high-probability guarantee. LTT, though, achieves high-probability risk control but is much more conservative because it uses concentration inequalities. Monotonized-loss CRC is conservative due to Jensen’s inequality: monotonizing each loss is far more conservative than monotonizing the empirical risk even though it is only considering risk control in expectation.

Note that the LTT is designed for i.i.d. data and may fail when distribution shift or feedback covariate shift exists. In the medical QA task, the policy is not updated, and no feedback covariate shift exists. In Appendix G.5, we provide additional analysis on LTT and another UCB-based method. We show that LTT may fail under covariate shift because it ignores the shift and can be overly conservative. A detailed comparison of our method with other high-probability risk control methods regarding conservatism and feedback covariate shift can be found in Appendix G.5.

5.3 Comparison of Weighted Risk Estimation Methods

Outperforming O-CRC with Importance Weights. O-CRC uses a self-normalized importance-weighting estimator to estimate risk and then applies risk control on top of it. Under a monotonic risk function, the difference between RCL-E and O-CRC is the weighting method, i.e., permutation weight vs. importance weight. The breast cancer results in Figure 1 show that our method achieves lower risk and stays below the target threshold throughout online learning, while O-CRC requires much more calibration data to reach the target risk level. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our permutation-based weight estimator. In Figure 3 (a) and (b), we see that our risk evaluator exhibits lower variance and bias than the standard importance-weighted method. This empirically demonstrates the lower-variance property.

Comparison of Weight Estimation Performances. We compare RCL-E with alternative approximations of the permutation marginal weights to show that our Sinkhorn approximation is effective. Specifically, we consider the multi-step estimator of Prinster et al. [6] in Figure 3 (c), which approximates the full permutation marginal by restricting the assignment space to the most recent positions; details are provided in Appendix G.3. Our method consistently achieves lower risk, showing the benefit of modeling the full permutation assignment, and our Sinkhorn method is an effective approximation. Moreover, as the multi-step window increases and better approximates the full assignment, its risk decreases and approaches that of our method.

5.4 Additional Ablation Studies

We analyze the Sinkhorn approximation error in Appendix G.6.1 and provide empirical and theoretical analysis of how this weight-approximation error affects the theoretical guarantee in Appendix G.6.2. We also empirically verify the assumption that the log range does not increase in Appendix G.6.3 and empirically verify Theorem 4.5 and its assumptions in Appendix G.6.4.

6 Conclusion

In our work, we present a high-probability risk control method using a permutation-based weighted risk evaluator that employs the Sinkhorn approximation to compute the permutation marginal weight. Theoretically, we show that our method has no larger worst-case variance than the standard importance-weighted method. We also show that our policy selection method achieves asymptotic high-probability risk control. Empirically, we validate our claim that our methods achieve high-probability risk control in safe bandit, safe question answering, and medical QA tasks. We also validated that our efficient risk evaluator outperforms baselines in expected risk control. Future work includes extending the framework to safe LLM reasoning and safe exploration in RL.

Appendix A Related Work

Standard Conformal Prediction and Risk Control for Exchangeable Data

Conformal prediction (CP) is a framework for quantifying uncertainty in machine learning that uses calibration data to turn point predictions into valid, rigorously calibrated prediction sets or intervals. The classic textbook reference for CP and related methods is Vovk et al. [10], but also see Angelopoulos et al. [23] for a more modern textbook and Angelopoulos and Bates [24] for a gentle introduction to CP. Standard CP methods generally assume that the calibration and test data are exchangeable, meaning that their joint distribution is invariant to permutations. Informally, exchangeability means the distribution is unchanging across deployment environments and across time; for example, independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data are the most common example of exchangeable data. Angelopoulos et al. [4] introduced conformal risk control (CRC), an extension of conformal prediction to control the expected value of any loss function that is monotonically parameterized by a control parameter, λ\lambda. CRC recovers standard CP when the loss function in question is a miscoverage indicator and the tuning parameter controls the size of the prediction set. For example, CRC can be used to control the false negative rate in multilabel classification, where the tuning parameter controls the size of the prediction set.

Weighted Conformal Prediction for Adapting to Fixed Distribution Shifts

Tibshirani et al. [8] introduced weighted conformal prediction (WCP) to extend CP to adapt to a fixed covariate shift between a source and target distribution. That is, WCP uses the likelihood ratio between the source and target distribution to reweight calibration data and attain CP’s coverage guarantee even under such covariate shift. More broadly, WCP in Tibshirani et al. [8] applies to data that are weighted exchangeable, as defined in that paper. Fannjiang et al. [5] extended WCP to allow for a single round of feedback covariate shift (FCS), where a single target distribution depends on data from a single source distribution. Prinster et al. [25], Prinster et al. [26] developed cross-validation style WCP methods for standard covariate shift and FCS. Nair and Janson [9] studied WCP under multiple rounds of FCS and Stanton et al. [27] applied WCP to multiround Bayesian optimization similar to the online policy learning setting in our paper, but noted gaps in the theory. Prinster et al. [6] demonstrated and explained how WCP can theoretically generalize to any data distribution, a practical focus on multiround FCS induced by online policy learning in black-box optimization and active learning. Relevant to the risk evaluation contribution of our paper, several works have leveraged ideas from WCP for off-policy prediction or evaluation in an offline setting [28, 29, 30]. However, these works differ from our focus on an online setting with FCS. Also relevant are the fixed-weight CP methods of Barber et al. [31], which characterize a worst-case “coverage gap,” and the unifying perspective in Barber and Tibshirani [32]. We also note that CRC [4] allows for weighted extensions to adapt to standard covariate shift. This whole line of literature, however, focuses on developing WCP algorithms for adapting to distribution shifts that are fixed ahead of time, whether by the environment or a pre-defined learning procedure; in other words, these works do not consider selecting a policy to respect a risk constraint.

Conformal Policy Control for Selecting a Risk-Controlling Policy

Most relevant to our current paper, Prinster et al. [3] introduce conformal policy control (CPC) as a framework for selecting a policy that is optimized but still controlling a given risk constraint in expectation. In contrast to classic conservative optimization methods that generally treat the search for a risk-controlling policy as a hyperparameter tuning problem (e.g., tuning the regularization strength to find an adequate divergence penalty), CPC and our paper circumvent such hyperparameter tuning by directly prescribing a risk-controlling policy to meet a user’s declared risk tolerance. CPC achieves this prescriptive use case by extending CRC [4] in two main ways: (i) to allow the tuning parameter to control the policy rather than the loss; and (ii) to allow for non-monotonicity via a more conservative selection criterion. As described in the main text, however, CPC has at least two limitations that we aim to address in the current paper. First, CPC’s guarantees hold for exact permutation weights (from Prinster et al. [6]). Still, the CPC paper [3] does not theoretically characterize any relation between its practical weight estimation and exact permutation weights. To address this limitation, we propose an efficient method based on the Sinkhorn algorithm to estimate permutation marginal probability weights, and we show that permutation weights yield a lower worst-case variance than sample-wise importance weights (which can fail in FCS). Second, the CPC guarantee controls risk in expectation (as in CRC), which can fail to control risk for a given policy deployment if variance is high. To address this second limitation, we instead focus on (asymptotic) high-probability risk control, which can (asymptotically) assure that a given policy deployment is likely safe.

High-Probability Risk Control

Much of the existing work on high-probability risk control assumes exchangeable or i.i.d. data [11, 12]. However, such assumptions are often violated in adaptive decision-making settings, where the data collection process evolves with the policy itself. Fannjiang and Park [33] study reliable algorithm selection with high-probability guarantees under distribution shift, but in practice they require density-ratio estimation so the guarantees may not directly apply due to estimation error. Existing high-probability approaches also typically require multiple testing corrections [11, 12, 33], which can become overly conservative. For example, Learn-then-Test achieves an overall error level δ\delta by requiring each hypothesis test to pass at a much smaller level, e.g., δ/|Λ|\delta/|\Lambda|, which can be prohibitively conservative when the candidate family |Λ||\Lambda| is large. In contrast, our method develops an asymptotic high-probability risk-control framework based on simultaneous bootstrap correction, which directly accounts for the selection effect while yielding less conservative risk control.

Permutation Marginal Weight Approximation

Recent works on conformal prediction and risk control interpret conformal methods through permutation testing under distribution shift. However, computing exact permutation marginals quickly becomes intractable as the number of observations grows. Tibshirani et al. [8] acknowledge the computational challenge associated with computing conformal weights for complicated cases of weighted exchangeable data, although they limited their practical focus to the relatively simple case of standard covariate shift, where a single source distribution is independent of a single target distribution. Prinster et al. [6] use a surrogate approximation that considers only the permutation assignment at the most recent position, which may introduce additional approximation bias. Prinster et al. [3] further propose an averaged weighting approximation for policy control under adaptive data collection that treats past observations as sampled exchangeably from the mixture distribution of past policies. Nair and Janson [9] and Barber and Tibshirani [32] propose using Monte Carlo randomization methods to estimate permutation weights, but these randomization approaches generally suffer from high variance. To obtain a more accurate and scalable approximation, we build on ideas from permutation marginal inference and entropy-regularized optimization over the Birkhoff polytope. In particular, Mena et al. [14] propose a Sinkhorn variational relaxation that replaces the intractable permutation entropy with a tractable entrywise entropy surrogate, leading to efficient matrix-scaling algorithms based on Sinkhorn iterations [7]. Inspired by this line of work, we use a Sinkhorn-based approximation to efficiently estimate permutation marginal weights induced by adaptive policy assignments under feedback covariate shift.

Also, the quantile-based methods such as [34] predict the adaptive quantile for the regression and VaR, and CVaR [35, 36] predict the statistical confidence bound of the risk. Our work focuses on expected policy risk under FCS, with bootstrap quantiles describing joint estimation error rather than the tail of individual losses. Another related line of work is model-based OPE. OPE includes outcome-model estimators, sequential doubly robust estimators, and model-based bootstrap confidence bounds [37, 38, 39]. These provide alternative approaches to risk estimation, while our method uses permutation weighting without a separate outcome model and studies calibration for risk-constrained policy selection under a feedback-dependent sampling process. Randomization tests and generalized conformal weighting handle adaptive sampling [9]. Our method shares this likelihood-based foundation but targets expected-loss calibration and uses Sinkhorn approximations for the weights instead of randomization tests or Monte Carlo bootstrapping for permutation estimation.

Appendix C More Details on Permutation Marginal Weights

C.1 Permutation Marginal Weight Calculation

In this section, we derive the permutation marginal weight pi​(λ)p_{i}(\lambda) using the law of total probability. Let

EZ:={Z1,…,Zt+1}E_{Z}:=\{Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{t+1}\}

denote the unordered bag of observed data, and let Z^t+1\hat{Z}_{t+1} denote the random sample assigned to the final position under a random ordering. Then

ℙ⁡(Z^t+1=Zi∣EZ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigl(\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i}\mid E_{Z}\bigr) =ℙ⁡(Z^t+1=Zi,EZ)ℙ⁡(EZ)\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{P}\bigl(\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i},E_{Z}\bigr)}{\mathbb{P}(E_{Z})}
=∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=iπ(zσ⁡(1),…,zσ⁡(t+1))∑σπ⁡(zσ⁡(1),…,zσ⁡(t+1)).\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(t+1)=i}\pi\bigl(z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,z_{\sigma(t+1)}\bigr)}{\sum_{\sigma}\pi\bigl(z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,z_{\sigma(t+1)}\bigr)}. (C.1)

Here, σ\sigma ranges over all permutations of {1,…,t+1}\{1,\ldots,t+1\}, and σ⁡(t+1)=i\sigma(t+1)=i means that sample ii is assigned to the final position. The term π⁡(zσ⁡(1),…,zσ⁡(t+1))\pi(z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,z_{\sigma(t+1)}) denotes the joint density of the data under the ordering σ\sigma. Under exchangeability,

π⁡(zσ⁡(1),…,zσ⁡(t+1))=π⁡(z1,…,zt+1)\pi(z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,z_{\sigma(t+1)})=\pi(z_{1},\ldots,z_{t+1})

for all σ\sigma, and the marginal weights reduce to uniform weights.

Under MFCS for contextual bandits, following Prinster et al. [6], the joint density can be factorized into time-dependent and time-invariant terms:

π⁡(Z1,…,Zt+1)\displaystyle\pi(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{t+1}) =∏j=1t+1p(Aj,Xj∣Z1,…,Zj−1)⏟time-dependent​∏j=1t+1p⁡(Lj∣Xj,Aj)⏟invariant\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}\underbrace{p(A_{j},X_{j}\mid Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{j-1})}_{\text{time-dependent}}\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}\underbrace{p(L_{j}\mid X_{j},A_{j})}_{\text{invariant}}
=∏j=1t+1p⁡(Aj∣Z1,…,Zj−1,Xj)⏟policy-dependent​∏j=1t+1pX​(Xj)​∏j=1t+1p⁡(Lj∣Xj,Aj)⏟invariant.\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}\underbrace{p(A_{j}\mid Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{j-1},X_{j})}_{\text{policy-dependent}}\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}p_{X}(X_{j})\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}\underbrace{p(L_{j}\mid X_{j},A_{j})}_{\text{invariant}}. (C.2)

In the permutation ratio in Eq.(C.1), the context density ∏j=1t+1pX​(Xj)\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}p_{X}(X_{j}) and the loss conditional density ∏j=1t+1p⁡(Lj∣Xj,Aj)\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}p(L_{j}\mid X_{j},A_{j}) are invariant to the ordering and cancel between numerator and denominator. Therefore, only the policy-dependent terms remain. Plugging Eq.(C.2) into Eq.(C.1) gives

ℙ(Z^t+1=Zi∣EZ)=∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=i∏j=1t+1p(Aσ⁡(j)∣Zσ⁡(1),…,Zσ⁡(j−1),Xσ⁡(j))∑σ∏j=1t+1p⁡(Aσ⁡(j)∣Zσ⁡(1),…,Zσ⁡(j−1),Xσ⁡(j)).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigl(\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i}\mid E_{Z}\bigr)=\frac{\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(t+1)=i}\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}p\bigl(A_{\sigma(j)}\mid Z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,Z_{\sigma(j-1)},X_{\sigma(j)}\bigr)}{\sum_{\sigma}\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}p\bigl(A_{\sigma(j)}\mid Z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,Z_{\sigma(j-1)},X_{\sigma(j)}\bigr)}. (C.3)

Computing Eq.(C.3) exactly would require re-learning the policy for every prefix of every permutation, which is infeasible. We therefore use a fixed learned-policy-sequence approximation: the learned policies are held fixed, and only the observed data points are permuted. Let

πθ,λ1,…,πθ,λt,πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1},\ldots,\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t},\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}

denote the fixed policy sequence, where πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1} is the candidate deployment policy for the final position. Then the permutation marginal weight is approximated by

pi(λ):=ℙ(Z^t+1=Zi∣EZ,λ)≈∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=i∏j=1t+1πθ,λj(Aσ⁡(j)∣Xσ⁡(j))∑σ∏j=1t+1πθ,λj​(Aσ⁡(j)∣Xσ⁡(j)).\displaystyle p_{i}(\lambda):=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i}\mid E_{Z},\lambda\bigr)\approx\frac{\sum_{\sigma:\sigma(t+1)=i}\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{j}\bigl(A_{\sigma(j)}\mid X_{\sigma(j)}\bigr)}{\sum_{\sigma}\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{j}\bigl(A_{\sigma(j)}\mid X_{\sigma(j)}\bigr)}. (C.4)

C.2 Proof of Proposition 3.3: Reduction to SNIPS

We show that, under standard covariate shift, the exact permutation marginal weight reduces to the self-normalized importance sampling (SNIPS) weight. Suppose all historical data are collected by a fixed behavior policy πb\pi_{b}, and the next-round risk is evaluated under the target policy πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}.

We first write the probability that the final position is occupied by the observed data point Zi=(Xi,Ai,Ri,Li)Z_{i}=(X_{i},A_{i},R_{i},L_{i}). Under a fixed behavior policy πb\pi_{b} for the first tt positions and the target policy πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1} for the (t+1)(t+1)-th position, we have

ℙ(Z^t+1=Zi∣EZ,λ)=∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=i[∏k=1tπb(Aσ⁡(k)∣Xσ⁡(k))]πθ,λt+1(Ai∣Xi)∏h=1t+1pX(Xh)𝒵,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i}\mid E_{Z},\lambda)=\frac{\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(t+1)=i}\left[\prod_{k=1}^{t}\pi_{b}(A_{\sigma(k)}\mid X_{\sigma(k)})\right]\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})\prod_{h=1}^{t+1}p_{X}(X_{h})}{\mathcal{Z}}, (C.5)

where 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is the normalizing constant. Since ∏h=1t+1pX​(Xh)\prod_{h=1}^{t+1}p_{X}(X_{h}) does not depend on the permutation, it cancels after normalization. Moreover, conditional on Z^t+1=Zi\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i}, the remaining tt observations can be assigned to the first tt positions in t!t! possible ways. Therefore,

ℙ⁡(Z^t+1=Zi∣EZ,λ)=t!​πθ,λt+1​(Ai∣Xi)​∏j≠it+1πb​(Aj∣Xj)𝒵.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i}\mid E_{Z},\lambda)=\frac{t!\,\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})\prod_{j\neq i}^{t+1}\pi_{b}(A_{j}\mid X_{j})}{\mathcal{Z}}. (C.6)

The normalizing constant is obtained by summing over all possible choices of the observation assigned to the final position:

𝒵=∑ℓ=1t+1t!​πθ,λt+1​(Aℓ∣Xℓ)​∏j≠ℓt+1πb​(Aj∣Xj).\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{t+1}t!\,\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{\ell}\mid X_{\ell})\prod_{j\neq\ell}^{t+1}\pi_{b}(A_{j}\mid X_{j}). (C.7)

Hence,

ℙ⁡(Z^t+1=Zi∣EZ,λ)=πθ,λt+1​(Ai∣Xi)​∏j≠it+1πb​(Aj∣Xj)∑ℓ=1t+1πθ,λt+1​(Aℓ∣Xℓ)​∏j≠ℓt+1πb​(Aj∣Xj).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i}\mid E_{Z},\lambda)=\frac{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})\prod_{j\neq i}^{t+1}\pi_{b}(A_{j}\mid X_{j})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{\ell}\mid X_{\ell})\prod_{j\neq\ell}^{t+1}\pi_{b}(A_{j}\mid X_{j})}. (C.8)

Dividing both the numerator and denominator by ∏j=1t+1πb​(Aj∣Xj)\prod_{j=1}^{t+1}\pi_{b}(A_{j}\mid X_{j}) gives

ℙ⁡(Z^t+1=Zi∣EZ,λ)=πθ,λt+1​(Ai∣Xi)/πb​(Ai∣Xi)∑ℓ=1t+1πθ,λt+1​(Aℓ∣Xℓ)/πb​(Aℓ∣Xℓ).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\hat{Z}_{t+1}=Z_{i}\mid E_{Z},\lambda)=\frac{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})/\pi_{b}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{\ell}\mid X_{\ell})/\pi_{b}(A_{\ell}\mid X_{\ell})}. (C.9)

Therefore, the permutation marginal probability of assigning ZiZ_{i} to the (t+1)(t+1)-th position coincides with the SNIPS weight.

C.3 Proof of Proposition 3.4: A Global Importance Weight

The proof is straightforward. From Eq.(C.4), under the fixed policy sequence πθ,λ1,…,πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{1},\ldots,\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}, we have

pi​(λ)\displaystyle p_{i}(\lambda) =∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=i∏h=1t+1πθ,λh(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h))∑σ∏h=1t+1πθ,λh​(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h)).\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(t+1)=i}\prod_{h=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr)}{\sum_{\sigma}\prod_{h=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr)}. (C.10)

The numerator corresponds to the total likelihood of all permutations in which sample ii is assigned to the (t+1)(t+1)-th position. Therefore, it can be written as

∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=i∏h=1t+1πθ,λh(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h))\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(t+1)=i}\prod_{h=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr)
=∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=iπθ,λt+1(Ai∣Xi)∏h=1tπθ,λh(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h))\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(t+1)=i}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}\bigl(A_{i}\mid X_{i}\bigr)\prod_{h=1}^{t}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr)
=πθ,λt+1(Ai∣Xi)∑σ:σ⁡(t+1)=i∏h=1tπθ,λh(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h)).\displaystyle\qquad=\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}\bigl(A_{i}\mid X_{i}\bigr)\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(t+1)=i}\prod_{h=1}^{t}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr). (C.11)

Similarly, the denominator is the total likelihood over all permutations. We decompose it according to the position k∈{1,…,t+1}k\in\{1,\ldots,t+1\} occupied by sample ii:

∑σ∏h=1t+1πθ,λh​(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h))\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma}\prod_{h=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr)
=∑k=1t+1∑σ:σ⁡(k)=i∏h=1t+1πθ,λh(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h))\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{k=1}^{t+1}\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(k)=i}\prod_{h=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr)
=∑k=1t+1πθ,λk(Ai∣Xi)∑σ:σ⁡(k)=i∏h=1h≠kt+1πθ,λh(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h)).\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{k=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{k}\bigl(A_{i}\mid X_{i}\bigr)\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(k)=i}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}h=1\\ h\neq k\end{subarray}}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr). (C.12)

Define

Ci,k:=∑σ:σ⁡(k)=i∏h=1h≠kt+1πθ,λh(Aσ⁡(h)∣Xσ⁡(h)).\displaystyle C_{i,k}:=\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(k)=i}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}h=1\\ h\neq k\end{subarray}}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{h}\bigl(A_{\sigma(h)}\mid X_{\sigma(h)}\bigr). (C.13)

Then the numerator in Eq.(C.11) is

πθ,λt+1​(Ai∣Xi)​Ci,t+1,\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})C_{i,t+1},

and the denominator in Eq.(C.12) is

∑k=1t+1πθ,λk​(Ai∣Xi)​Ci,k.\sum_{k=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{k}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})C_{i,k}.

Therefore,

pi​(λ)\displaystyle p_{i}(\lambda) =πθ,λt+1​(Ai∣Xi)​Ci,t+1∑k=1t+1πθ,λk​(Ai∣Xi)​Ci,k.\displaystyle=\frac{\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})C_{i,t+1}}{\sum_{k=1}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{k}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})C_{i,k}}. (C.14)

This shows that the permutation marginal weight can be interpreted as a global importance-weighting method: the weight assigned to sample ii depends not only on the likelihood of observing AiA_{i} under the target policy πθ,λt+1\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{t+1}, but also on the global compatibility factors Ci,kC_{i,k}, which aggregate over all feasible assignments of the remaining samples to the remaining positions.

C.4 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Lemma C.1 (Variational representation of log-sum-exp / Gibbs variational principle).

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be a finite set of permutations, and let f:𝒮→ℝf:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R} be any function. Let μ⁡(σ)\mu(\sigma) denote a probability distribution over permutations σ∈𝒮\sigma\in\mathcal{S}. Then

log∑σ∈𝒮ef⁡(σ)=maxμ∈𝒫⁡(𝒮){∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)f(σ)+H(μ)},\log\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}e^{f(\sigma)}=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})}\left\{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)f(\sigma)+H(\mu)\right\},

where

𝒫(𝒮)={μ:μ(σ)≥0,∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)=1}\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})=\left\{\mu:\mu(\sigma)\geq 0,\ \sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)=1\right\}

is the probability simplex and

H(μ)=−∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)logμ(σ)H(\mu)=-\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)\log\mu(\sigma)

is the Shannon entropy. Moreover, the maximizer is

μ∗​(σ)=ef⁡(σ)∑σ′∈𝒮ef⁡(σ′).\mu^{*}(\sigma)=\frac{e^{f(\sigma)}}{\sum_{\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}e^{f(\sigma^{\prime})}}.
Proof of Lemma C.1.

Let

Z:=∑σ∈𝒮ef⁡(σ),μ∗​(σ):=ef⁡(σ)Z.Z:=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}e^{f(\sigma)},\qquad\mu^{*}(\sigma):=\frac{e^{f(\sigma)}}{Z}.

For any μ∈𝒫⁡(𝒮)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}), the Kullback–Leibler divergence satisfies

KL(μ∥μ∗)≥0,\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|\mu^{*})\geq 0,

with equality if and only if μ=μ∗\mu=\mu^{*}. Expanding,

KL(μ∥μ∗)=∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)logμ⁡(σ)μ∗​(σ)=∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)logμ(σ)−∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)(f(σ)−logZ).\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|\mu^{*})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)\log\frac{\mu(\sigma)}{\mu^{*}(\sigma)}=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)\log\mu(\sigma)-\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)\big(f(\sigma)-\log Z\big).

Rearranging gives

logZ=∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)f(σ)−∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)logμ(σ)+KL(μ∥μ∗).\log Z=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)f(\sigma)-\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)\log\mu(\sigma)+\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|\mu^{*}).

Since

H(μ)=−∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)logμ(σ)H(\mu)=-\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)\log\mu(\sigma)

and KL(μ∥μ∗)≥0\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|\mu^{*})\geq 0, we obtain

∑σ∈𝒮μ⁡(σ)​f​(σ)+H⁡(μ)≤log⁡Z,\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)f(\sigma)+H(\mu)\leq\log Z,

with equality when μ=μ∗\mu=\mu^{*}. Therefore,

log∑σ∈𝒮ef⁡(σ)=maxμ∈𝒫⁡(𝒮){∑σ∈𝒮μ(σ)f(σ)+H(μ)}.\log\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}e^{f(\sigma)}=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S})}\left\{\sum_{\sigma\in\mathcal{S}}\mu(\sigma)f(\sigma)+H(\mu)\right\}.

∎

Remark C.2 (Interpretation of the Gibbs variational principle).

The Gibbs variational principle shows that the log-sum-exp over all permutations can be viewed as an optimization over probability distributions on permutations. In our setting, each permutation σ\sigma corresponds to a possible assignment of observed samples to time positions, and f⁡(σ)f(\sigma) is the log-likelihood score for that ordering. The maximizer

μ∗​(σ)=ef⁡(σ)∑σ′∈𝒮ef⁡(σ′)\mu^{*}(\sigma)=\frac{e^{f(\sigma)}}{\sum_{\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{S}}e^{f(\sigma^{\prime})}}

is therefore the normalized Gibbs distribution over permutations. This provides a probabilistic interpretation of the exact permutation distribution: orderings with larger likelihood scores receive larger probability. At the same time, the entropy term H⁡(μ)H(\mu) prevents the variational problem from collapsing onto a single highest-scoring permutation. The main computational difficulty is that μ∗\mu^{*} is defined over all permutations, whose number grows factorially. This motivates replacing the full distribution over permutations by a tractable marginal assignment matrix and approximating its entropy using a marginal-entropy relaxation.

Lemma C.3 (Expected score expressed by the marginal matrix).

Let μ\mu be a probability distribution over permutations σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n}, and define

f⁡(σ):=∑i=1nlog⁡Ji,σ⁡(i),f(\sigma):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log J_{i,\sigma(i)},

where J∈ℝ+n×nJ\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n\times n}. Define the marginal assignment matrix.

Qi​j:=Prμ(σ(i)=j)=∑σ:σ⁡(i)=jμ(σ).Q_{ij}:=\Pr_{\mu}\!\left(\sigma(i)=j\right)=\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(i)=j}\mu(\sigma).

Then

𝔼μ​[f⁡(σ)]=∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​j​log⁡Ji​j.\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\!\left[f(\sigma)\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log J_{ij}.
Proof of Lemma C.3.

By definition,

𝔼μ​[f⁡(σ)]=∑σ∈Snμ⁡(σ)​f​(σ)=∑σ∈Snμ⁡(σ)​∑i=1nlog⁡Ji,σ⁡(i).\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[f(\sigma)]=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\mu(\sigma)f(\sigma)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\mu(\sigma)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log J_{i,\sigma(i)}.

Interchanging the order of summation gives

𝔼μ​[f⁡(σ)]=∑i=1n∑σ∈Snμ⁡(σ)​log⁡Ji,σ⁡(i).\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[f(\sigma)]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\mu(\sigma)\log J_{i,\sigma(i)}.

For a fixed ii, we group permutations according to the value of σ⁡(i)\sigma(i):

∑σ∈Snμ(σ)logJi,σ⁡(i)=∑j=1n∑σ:σ⁡(i)=jμ(σ)logJi​j.\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\mu(\sigma)\log J_{i,\sigma(i)}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(i)=j}\mu(\sigma)\log J_{ij}.

Since log⁡Ji​j\log J_{ij} is constant over all permutations satisfying σ⁡(i)=j\sigma(i)=j, we obtain

∑σ∈Snμ(σ)logJi,σ⁡(i)=∑j=1nlogJi​j∑σ:σ⁡(i)=jμ(σ)=∑j=1nQi​jlogJi​j.\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\mu(\sigma)\log J_{i,\sigma(i)}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\log J_{ij}\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(i)=j}\mu(\sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log J_{ij}.

Summing over ii yields

𝔼μ​[f⁡(σ)]=∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​j​log⁡Ji​j,\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[f(\sigma)]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log J_{ij},

which completes the proof. ∎

Remark C.4.

Lemma C.3 shows that the expected log-score of a distribution over permutations depends on μ\mu only through its marginal assignment matrix QQ. Thus, the likelihood part of the variational objective can be expressed directly in terms of QQ, even though the entropy term H⁡(μ)H(\mu) still depends on the full distribution over permutations. This key step motivates replacing the intractable optimization over permutation distributions with a tractable relaxation over doubly stochastic matrices.

Now we prove Theorem 3.1.

Proof.

The permanent of JJ is defined as

Z=perm⁡(J)=∑σ∈Sn∏i=1nJi,σ⁡(i),\displaystyle Z=\operatorname{perm}(J)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}J_{i,\sigma(i)}, (C.15)

where σ\sigma denotes a permutation of {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}.

Define the log-score of a permutation σ\sigma as

f(σ)=log∏i=1nJi,σ⁡(i)=∑i=1nlogJi,σ⁡(i).f(\sigma)=\log\prod_{i=1}^{n}J_{i,\sigma(i)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log J_{i,\sigma(i)}.

Then the log-permanent can be written as the log-sum-exp over all permutations:

logperm(J)=log∑σ∈Snef⁡(σ).\displaystyle\log\operatorname{perm}(J)=\log\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}e^{f(\sigma)}. (C.16)

Then, using Lemma C.1 and Lemma C.3, we can rewrite the log-permanent as

log⁡Z=log⁡perm⁡(J)\displaystyle\log Z=\log\operatorname{perm}(J) =log∑σ∈Snef⁡(σ)\displaystyle=\log\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}e^{f(\sigma)} (C.17)
=maxμ∈𝒫⁡(Sn)⁡{∑σ∈Snμ⁡(σ)​f​(σ)+H⁡(μ)}\displaystyle=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(S_{n})}\left\{\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\mu(\sigma)f(\sigma)+H(\mu)\right\} (C.18)
=maxμ∈𝒫⁡(Sn)⁡{∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​jμ​log⁡Ji​j+H⁡(μ)},\displaystyle=\max_{\mu\in\mathcal{P}(S_{n})}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}^{\mu}\log J_{ij}+H(\mu)\right\}, (C.19)

where

Qi​jμ=Prμ⁡(σ⁡(i)=j)Q_{ij}^{\mu}=\Pr_{\mu}\!\left(\sigma(i)=j\right)

is the marginal assignment matrix induced by the distribution μ\mu over permutations.

The entropy term H⁡(μ)H(\mu) is defined on the full distribution over permutations and cannot, in general, be written exactly as a function of the marginal matrix QQ alone. We therefore use a marginal-entropy relaxation, replacing H⁡(μ)H(\mu) by the entrywise entropy of QQ:

H(μ)≈H(Q)=−∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​jlogQi​j.H(\mu)\approx H(Q)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log Q_{ij}.

This gives the tractable approximation

log⁡Z=log⁡perm⁡(J)\displaystyle\log Z=\log\operatorname{perm}(J) ≈maxQ∈Bn⁡{∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​j​log⁡Ji​j−∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​j​log⁡Qi​j}\displaystyle\approx\max_{Q\in B_{n}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log J_{ij}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log Q_{ij}\right\} (C.20)
=maxQ∈Bn{−∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​jlogQi​jJi​j}\displaystyle=\max_{Q\in B_{n}}\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log\frac{Q_{ij}}{J_{ij}}\right\} (C.21)
=−minQ∈BnKL(Q∥J),\displaystyle=-\min_{Q\in B_{n}}\mathrm{KL}(Q\|J), (C.22)

where

Bn={Q∈ℝ+n×n:Q𝟏=𝟏,Q⊤𝟏=𝟏}B_{n}=\left\{Q\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n\times n}:Q\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},\ Q^{\top}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}\right\}

is the Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices.

Equivalently, the approximate marginal assignment matrix is obtained by solving

Q⋆=argminQ∈BnKL(Q∥J).Q^{\star}=\arg\min_{Q\in B_{n}}\mathrm{KL}(Q\|J).

The last row of Q⋆Q^{\star} is then used as the approximation to the permutation marginal weights:

pi(λ)≈Qn,i⋆,i=1,…,n.p_{i}(\lambda)\approx Q^{\star}_{n,i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.

∎

C.5 Optimization with Sinkhorn algorithm

Consider the entropy-regularized assignment problem

Q⋆=argminQ∈BnKL(Q∥J),Q^{\star}=\arg\min_{Q\in B_{n}}\mathrm{KL}(Q\|J),

where

Bn={Q∈ℝ+n×n:∑j=1nQi​j=1,∑i=1nQi​j=1}B_{n}=\left\{Q\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n\times n}:\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}Q_{ij}=1\right\}

is the set of doubly stochastic matrices, and

KL(Q∥J):=∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​jlogQi​jJi​j.\mathrm{KL}(Q\|J):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log\frac{Q_{ij}}{J_{ij}}.

Here, J∈ℝ+n×nJ\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n\times n} is the stage–sample score matrix.

We introduce Lagrange multipliers {λi}i=1n\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} and {ηj}j=1n\{\eta_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n} for the row- and column-sum constraints, respectively. The Lagrangian is

ℒ⁡(Q,λ,η)=∑i=1n∑j=1nQi​j​log⁡Qi​jJi​j+∑i=1nλi​(∑j=1nQi​j−1)+∑j=1nηj​(∑i=1nQi​j−1).\mathcal{L}(Q,\lambda,\eta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}\log\frac{Q_{ij}}{J_{ij}}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}Q_{ij}-1\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta_{j}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}Q_{ij}-1\right).

Taking the partial derivative with respect to Qi​jQ_{ij} gives

∂ℒ∂Qi​j=log⁡Qi​j+1−log⁡Ji​j+λi+ηj.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial Q_{ij}}=\log Q_{ij}+1-\log J_{ij}+\lambda_{i}+\eta_{j}.

At an interior optimum, setting this derivative to zero yields

log⁡Qi​j=log⁡Ji​j−1−λi−ηj.\log Q_{ij}=\log J_{ij}-1-\lambda_{i}-\eta_{j}.

Equivalently,

Qi​j=ui​Ji​j​vj,Q_{ij}=u_{i}J_{ij}v_{j},

where

ui=e−1−λi,vj=e−ηj.u_{i}=e^{-1-\lambda_{i}},\qquad v_{j}=e^{-\eta_{j}}.

Therefore, any interior stationary point has the matrix-scaling form

Q=diag⁡(u)​J​diag⁡(v).Q=\operatorname{diag}(u)\,J\,\operatorname{diag}(v).

The scaling vectors uu and vv are chosen so that QQ satisfies the row- and column-sum constraints:

∑j=1nui​Ji​j​vj=1,∑i=1nui​Ji​j​vj=1.\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{i}J_{ij}v_{j}=1,\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}J_{ij}v_{j}=1.

Equivalently, they satisfy the fixed-point equations.

ui=1∑j=1nJi​j​vj,vj=1∑i=1nui​Ji​j.u_{i}=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}J_{ij}v_{j}},\qquad v_{j}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}J_{ij}}.

These equations motivate the Sinkhorn updates:

ui(k+1)=1∑j=1nJi​j​vj(k),vj(k+1)=1∑i=1nui(k+1)​Ji​j.u_{i}^{(k+1)}=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}J_{ij}v_{j}^{(k)}},\qquad v_{j}^{(k+1)}=\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}^{(k+1)}J_{ij}}.

If JJ has strictly positive entries, the Sinkhorn–Knopp theorem guarantees that such positive scaling factors exist and are unique up to a global multiplicative constant. Thus, alternating row and column normalization converges to the unique doubly stochastic matrix.

Q⋆=diag⁡(u)​J​diag⁡(v),Q^{\star}=\operatorname{diag}(u)\,J\,\operatorname{diag}(v),

which solves the above variational problem.

Appendix D Proof of Theorem 3.6

Proof.

By definition of TT and q1−δq_{1-\delta},

ℙ(∀λ∈Λ,ℓ(λ)−ℓ^(λ)≤q1−δ)≥1−δ.\mathbb{P}\left(\forall\lambda\in\Lambda,\;\ell(\lambda)-\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)\leq q_{1-\delta}\right)\geq 1-\delta.

On this event, for every λ∈Λ^feas\lambda\in\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}}, we have

ℓ⁡(λ)≤ℓ^​(λ)+q1−δ≤α,\ell(\lambda)\leq\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta}\leq\alpha,

where the last inequality follows from the definition

Λ^feas={λ∈Λ:ℓ^​(λ)+q1−δ≤α}.\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}}=\{\lambda\in\Lambda:\widehat{\ell}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta}\leq\alpha\}.

Therefore,

ℙ(∀λ∈Λ^feas,ℓ(λ)≤α)≥1−δ.\mathbb{P}\left(\forall\lambda\in\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}},\ell(\lambda)\leq\alpha\right)\geq 1-\delta.

Consequently, any policy selected from Λ^feas\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{feas}} also satisfies the risk constraint with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. ∎

Appendix E Proof of the worst-case variance

E.1 Proof of Proposition 4.1

Proof.

Since each of the mm actions has probability at least ϵ\epsilon, every relevant policy probability lies in [ϵ,1−(m−1)​ϵ][\epsilon,1-(m-1)\epsilon]. Hence Mϵ≥1M_{\epsilon}\geq 1, ΔJ≤log⁡Mϵ\Delta_{J}\leq\log M_{\epsilon}, and ωi≤Mϵ\omega_{i}\leq M_{\epsilon} for i≤ti\leq t. The probe ratio ωn=1\omega_{n}=1 satisfies the same bound, so maxi⁡ωi/n≤Mϵ/n=aIPS\max_{i}\omega_{i}/n\leq M_{\epsilon}/n=a_{\mathrm{IPS}}.

Let pmax=maxi⁡pip_{\max}=\max_{i}p_{i}. By the definition of Δp\Delta_{p}, pi≥pmax​e−Δpp_{i}\geq p_{\max}e^{-\Delta_{p}} for every ii. Since at least one coordinate equals pmaxp_{\max},

1=∑i=1npi≥pmax​[1+(n−1)​e−Δp].1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\geq p_{\max}\bigl[1+(n-1)e^{-\Delta_{p}}\bigr].

Using Δp≤ΔJ≤log⁡Mϵ\Delta_{p}\leq\Delta_{J}\leq\log M_{\epsilon} gives

Finally, Mϵ≥1M_{\epsilon}\geq 1 implies Mϵ+n−1≥nM_{\epsilon}+n-1\geq n, and therefore aperm≤aIPSa_{\mathrm{perm}}\leq a_{\mathrm{IPS}}. ∎

E.2 Proof of Theorem 4.3

Proof.

Let cc denote either pp or ω/n\omega/n, and put cmax=maxi⁡cic_{\max}=\max_{i}c_{i}. The weights are fixed, and the assumed moment bounds give, almost surely,
