Since Γn≥0\Gamma_{n}\geq 0 and 0≤aperm≤aIPS0\leq a_{\mathrm{perm}}\leq a_{\mathrm{IPS}}, we obtain Uperm≤UIPSU_{\mathrm{perm}}\leq U_{\mathrm{IPS}}. ∎

Appendix F Proof of Asymptotic high probability risk control

We first list the assumptions. For simplicity, we write bi​(A|X)b_{i}(A|X) for the policy at the ii-th step and qjq_{j} for the candidate policy for λj\lambda_{j}.

Assumption F.1.

Let 𝒳⊆ℝd\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be the context space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} a finite action space, and Λt+1={λ1,…,λK}\Lambda_{t+1}=\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{K}\} a fixed finite candidate family. Write bi​(A|X)b_{i}(A|X) for the policy at round ii and qjq_{j} for the candidate policy indexed by λj\lambda_{j}. Assume the following conditions:

  1. 1.

    Stable context and loss distributions. Let ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{i-1} denote the history available before round ii. Conditional on ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{i-1}, data are generated sequentially as

    Xi∼ν,Ai∼bi(⋅∣Xi).X_{i}\sim\nu,\qquad A_{i}\sim b_{i}(\cdot\mid X_{i}).

    The logging policy bib_{i} is ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{i-1}-measurable. The context distribution ν\nu and the conditional loss distribution remain fixed, with 0≤Li≤B0\leq L_{i}\leq B.

    Remark F.2.

    Contexts are i.i.d. and drawn from the same distribution, and the loss distribution remains unchanged for a given context-action pair. The logging policy bib_{i} may depend only on the history ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{i-1}.

  2. 2.

    Finite-dimensional affine policy. There exist ℱi−1\mathcal{F}_{i-1}-measurable vectors θi∈ℝr\theta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}, feature map f:𝒳×𝒜→ℝrf:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{r}, where supx,a‖f⁡(x,a)‖<∞\sup_{x,a}\|f(x,a)\|<\infty, a reference policy b⁡(a|x)b(a|x), such that the policy at each step bi​(a|x)b_{i}(a|x) can be represented as the affine structure of the reference policy:

    bi​(a∣x)=b⁡(a∣x)​{1+θi𝖳​f​(x,a)},∑a∈𝒜b⁡(a∣x)​f​(x,a)=0.b_{i}(a\mid x)=b(a\mid x)\{1+\theta_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}f(x,a)\},\qquad\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}b(a\mid x)f(x,a)=0.
    Remark F.3.

    There exists a reference policy b⁡(a|x)b(a|x), and the policy at each step is an affine transformation of the reference policy. The reference can be interpreted as the "averaging" policy that collects the historical data or the policy that the algorithm converges to. We want the policy to change smoothly and converge, so we use this affine structure to capture this pattern and property.

  3. 3.

    Mean-square stabilization. There exists a bounded deterministic sequence ai≥0a_{i}\geq 0 such that, almost surely,

    ‖θi‖≤ai,Δt:=1t​∑i=1tai2⟶0.\|\theta_{i}\|\leq a_{i},\qquad\Delta_{t}:=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}a_{i}^{2}\longrightarrow 0.
    Remark F.4.

    We first assume that the θi\theta_{i} is bounded, meaning that the deviation of the policy bi​(A|X)b_{i}(A|X) to the reference policy b⁡(A|X)b(A|X) is controlled and bounded. Δt\Delta_{t} converges to 00 when the policy converges to the reference policy. This assumption bounds the deviation of the logging policy from the reference policy and prevents unbounded, drastic policy changes.

  4. 4.

    Fixed candidates and uniform positivity. The number of candidates KK is fixed, and there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that, almost surely,

    b⁡(a∣x)≥ε,bi​(a∣x)≥ε,qj​(a∣x)≥εb(a\mid x)\geq\varepsilon,\qquad b_{i}(a\mid x)\geq\varepsilon,\qquad q_{j}(a\mid x)\geq\varepsilon

    for all i,j,x,ai,j,x,a, including possible test-point locations.

    Remark F.5.

    This is a general assumption that every action under every policy is chosen with at least ϵ\epsilon probability.

  5. 5.

    Nondegeneracy of the limiting scores. For each candidate λj\lambda_{j}, define

    gj​(X,A,L):=qj​(A∣X)b⁡(A∣X)​(L−ℓt+1​(λj)).g_{j}(X,A,L):=\frac{q_{j}(A\mid X)}{b(A\mid X)}\bigl(L-\ell_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})\bigr).

    Let 𝔼b\mathbb{E}_{b} denote expectation under X∼νX\sim\nu, A∣X∼b(⋅∣X)A\mid X\sim b(\cdot\mid X), and the fixed conditional loss distribution. Assume that

    min1≤j≤K⁡𝔼b​[gj​(X,A,L)2]>0.\min_{1\leq j\leq K}\mathbb{E}_{b}\!\left[g_{j}(X,A,L)^{2}\right]>0.
Remark F.6.

Assumption F.1 states the assumptions of the policy we will use in the following proof. Specifically, the policy depends only on historical data, and it is uniformly positive. The average squared deviation of the logging policies from the reference policy vanishes. Informally, the policy sequence changes smoothly and converges without extreme or drastic changes.

We now present three lemmas and their proofs. Lemma F.7 shows that the risk estimation error can be expanded as the first-order average of each observation’s error. Lemma F.9 shows that the covariance of the first-order terms converges to a fixed matrix. Lemma F.11 shows that the empirical first-order term used in our bootstrap algorithm converges to the theoretical first-order term in Lemma F.7.

Lemma F.7 (First-order expansion of the Sinkhorn risk estimator).

Under the first four conditions of Assumption F.1, consider the Sinkhorn estimator based on tt observations and a test point with assigned loss L~t+1=B\widetilde{L}_{t+1}=B, using exact doubly stochastic scaling. Define a reference policy bb.

For each λj∈Λt+1\lambda_{j}\in\Lambda_{t+1}, define

gj​(X,A,L)=qj​(A∣X)b⁡(A∣X)​(L−ℓt+1​(λj)),g_{j}(X,A,L)=\frac{q_{j}(A\mid X)}{b(A\mid X)}\bigl(L-\ell_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})\bigr),

and, for i≤ti\leq t, let

di,j=𝔼⁡[gj​(Xi,Ai,Li)∣ℱi−1],ψi​(λj)=gj​(Xi,Ai,Li)−di,j.d_{i,j}=\mathbb{E}[g_{j}(X_{i},A_{i},L_{i})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}],\qquad\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})=g_{j}(X_{i},A_{i},L_{i})-d_{i,j}.

These contributions are uniformly bounded and satisfy

𝔼⁡[ψi​(λj)∣ℱi−1]=0.\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=0.

Moreover,

ℓ^t+1​(λj)−ℓt+1​(λj)=1t+1​∑i=1tψi​(λj)+rt+1​(λj),\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})-\ell_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})=\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})+r_{t+1}(\lambda_{j}), (F.1)

where, for all sufficiently large tt,

(t+1)​𝔼​[∑j=1Krt+1​(λj)2]≤C⁡(Δt+t−1)⟶0.(t+1)\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{j=1}^{K}r_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})^{2}\right]\leq C\bigl(\Delta_{t}+t^{-1}\bigr)\longrightarrow 0.

Here CC is independent of tt. The effect of the test point is included in the remainder.

Remark F.8.

Lemma F.7 shows that the Sinkhorn risk estimation error can be represented by the summation of the error of each data point plus an average of negligible remainder. Under the mean-square stabilization assumption, the average logging policy b¯t=t−1​∑i=1tbi\bar{b}_{t}=t^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}b_{i} converges to the reference policy bb, which appears in the denominator of the first-order term. The remaining error is negligible at the t−1/2t^{-1/2} scale. This can be interpreted as viewing the historical data collected by an "average" policy, and estimating the risk with an importance-sampling estimator that uses such an "average" policy as the logging policy. Using the "average" policy and the importance-weight estimator induces a negligible error term at the t−1/2t^{-1/2} scale. We show empirically that the remainder term decreases to zero on a large dataset in Appendix G.6.4.

Proof Sketch: The proof begins by writing down the exact weight computed by the permutation and Sinkhorn algorithm. We first show that, replacing the exact weight with Sinkhorn with a simpler form, i.e. q⁡(Ak∣Xk)beff​(Ak∣Xk)\frac{q(A_{k}\mid X_{k})}{b_{\mathrm{eff}}(A_{k}\mid X_{k})}, where beffb_{\mathrm{eff}} is a weighted average of all the logging policies, changes the risk estimate at most at 1/t1/t scale. Then, we show that further replacing the weighted-average policy beffb_{\mathrm{eff}} with the averaging logging policy induces an error of at most t−1/2t^{-1/2} scale. And finally, by controlling the remainder, we prove the Lemma.

‖β−θ¯‖≤C​Δt​(‖β−θ¯‖+Ut+t−1).\|\beta-\bar{\theta}\|\leq C\Delta_{t}\bigl(\|\beta-\bar{\theta}\|+U_{t}+t^{-1}\bigr).

Lemma F.9 (Stabilization of the conditional covariance).

Under Assumption F.1, let

ψi=(ψi​(λ1),…,ψi​(λK))𝖳\psi_{i}=\bigl(\psi_{i}(\lambda_{1}),\ldots,\psi_{i}(\lambda_{K})\bigr)^{\mathsf{T}}

be the contributions defined in Lemma F.7. Define

Vj​k:=𝔼b​[gj​gk],Vt+1:=1t+1​∑i=1t𝔼⁡[ψi​ψi𝖳∣ℱi−1].V_{jk}:=\mathbb{E}_{b}[g_{j}g_{k}],\qquad V_{t+1}:=\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}].

Then VV is a deterministic positive semidefinite matrix with Vj​j>0V_{jj}>0 for every jj, and

‖Vt+1−V‖≤C⁡(Δt+Δt+t−1)⟶0almost surely.\|V_{t+1}-V\|\leq C\bigl(\sqrt{\Delta_{t}}+\Delta_{t}+t^{-1}\bigr)\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}.

In particular, Vt+1→𝑝VV_{t+1}\xrightarrow{p}V. Here ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes the operator norm and CC is independent of tt.

Remark F.10.

Lemma F.9 shows that the average covariance of the first-order terms described in Lemma F.7 converges to a fixed matrix VV, even though the policy changes over time. We empirically show that the covariance discrepancy decreases to zero with a large dataset in Appendix G.6.4.

Proof sketch: We can bound the difference of the VV, from reference policy, and Vt+1V_{t+1}, from data, by C⁡(‖θi‖+‖θi‖2)C(\|\theta_{i}\|+\|\theta_{i}\|^{2}), which is how far the policy at each step deviates from the reference policy. Although the policy at each step differs from the reference policy, the covariance difference is bounded by how far the policy deviates from the reference policy. Then, by averaging over all steps and using the mean-square stabilization assumption that bounds the deviation of the policy sequence, we obtain an entry-wise bound on the covariance.

Proof.

Recall that

hj=𝔼b​[f​gj],di,j=θi𝖳​hj,ψi​(λj)=gj​(Oi)−di,j,h_{j}=\mathbb{E}_{b}[fg_{j}],\qquad d_{i,j}=\theta_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{j},\qquad\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})=g_{j}(O_{i})-d_{i,j},

and

𝔼⁡[gj​(Oi)∣ℱi−1]=di,j.\mathbb{E}[g_{j}(O_{i})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=d_{i,j}.

Therefore, for every pair of candidates j,kj,k,

𝔼⁡[ψi​(λj)​ψi​(λk)∣ℱi−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})\psi_{i}(\lambda_{k})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]
=𝔼⁡[gj​(Oi)​gk​(Oi)∣ℱi−1]−di,j​di,k.\displaystyle\qquad=\mathbb{E}[g_{j}(O_{i})g_{k}(O_{i})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]-d_{i,j}d_{i,k}.

By the affine logging condition and the fixed context and conditional loss distributions,

𝔼⁡[gj​(Oi)​gk​(Oi)∣ℱi−1]=𝔼b​[(1+θi𝖳​f)​gj​gk].\mathbb{E}[g_{j}(O_{i})g_{k}(O_{i})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=\mathbb{E}_{b}[(1+\theta_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}f)g_{j}g_{k}].

Consequently,

𝔼⁡[ψi​(λj)​ψi​(λk)∣ℱi−1]−Vj​k\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})\psi_{i}(\lambda_{k})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]-V_{jk}
=θi𝖳​𝔼b​[f​gj​gk]−(θi𝖳​hj)​(θi𝖳​hk).\displaystyle\qquad=\theta_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbb{E}_{b}[fg_{j}g_{k}]-(\theta_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{j})(\theta_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{k}).

The functions f,gj,gkf,g_{j},g_{k} are uniformly bounded. Hence

|𝔼⁡[ψi​(λj)​ψi​(λk)∣ℱi−1]−Vj​k|≤C⁡(‖θi‖+‖θi‖2).\left|\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})\psi_{i}(\lambda_{k})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]-V_{jk}\right|\leq C\bigl(\|\theta_{i}\|+\|\theta_{i}\|^{2}\bigr).

The stabilization condition gives

1t​∑i=1t‖θi‖2≤Δt,1t​∑i=1t‖θi‖≤(1t​∑i=1t‖θi‖2)1/2≤Δt.\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\|\theta_{i}\|^{2}\leq\Delta_{t},\qquad\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\|\theta_{i}\|\leq\left(\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\|\theta_{i}\|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq\sqrt{\Delta_{t}}.

Thus

|1t​∑i=1t𝔼⁡[ψi​(λj)​ψi​(λk)∣ℱi−1]−Vj​k|≤C⁡(Δt+Δt).\left|\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})\psi_{i}(\lambda_{k})\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]-V_{jk}\right|\leq C(\sqrt{\Delta_{t}}+\Delta_{t}).

Since KK is fixed, the same bound holds in operator norm for the corresponding matrices.

Finally, changing the normalization from tt to t+1t+1 gives

Vt+1−V=tt+1​{1t​∑i=1t𝔼⁡[ψi​ψi𝖳∣ℱi−1]−V}−Vt+1.V_{t+1}-V=\frac{t}{t+1}\left\{\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]-V\right\}-\frac{V}{t+1}.

It follows that

‖Vt+1−V‖≤C⁡(Δt+Δt+t−1)⟶0almost surely.\|V_{t+1}-V\|\leq C(\sqrt{\Delta_{t}}+\Delta_{t}+t^{-1})\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{almost surely}.

The matrix VV is deterministic because the reference policy, candidate policies, and data-generating distributions are fixed. For every a∈ℝKa\in\mathbb{R}^{K},

a𝖳​V​a=𝔼b​[(∑j=1Kaj​gj)2]≥0.a^{\mathsf{T}}Va=\mathbb{E}_{b}\!\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^{K}a_{j}g_{j}\right)^{2}\right]\geq 0.

Thus VV is positive semidefinite. Its positive diagonal follows from the nondegeneracy condition in Assumption F.1. ∎

Under the first four conditions of Assumption F.1, define

ψ^i​(λj):=(t+1)​ϕ^i​(λj)=(t+1)​pi​(λj)​(L~i−ℓ^t+1​(λj)),\widehat{\psi}_{i}(\lambda_{j}):=(t+1)\widehat{\phi}_{i}(\lambda_{j})=(t+1)p_{i}(\lambda_{j})\bigl(\widetilde{L}_{i}-\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})\bigr),

where L~i=Li\widetilde{L}_{i}=L_{i} for i≤ti\leq t and L~t+1=B\widetilde{L}_{t+1}=B for the test point. Let

ψ^i=(ψ^i​(λ1),…,ψ^i​(λK))𝖳,\widehat{\psi}_{i}=\bigl(\widehat{\psi}_{i}(\lambda_{1}),\ldots,\widehat{\psi}_{i}(\lambda_{K})\bigr)^{\mathsf{T}},

and let ψi\psi_{i} be the real-data contributions from Lemma F.7.

Assigning zero ideal contribution to the test point, define

et+1 2:=1t+1​∑i=1t‖ψ^i−ψi‖2+1t+1​‖ψ^t+1‖2.e_{t+1}^{\,2}:=\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\|\widehat{\psi}_{i}-\psi_{i}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{t+1}\|\widehat{\psi}_{t+1}\|^{2}.

In particular, et+1 2→𝑝0e_{t+1}^{\,2}\xrightarrow{p}0.

Remark F.12.

In practice, we do not explicitly have the reference policy bb. So instead, we use ψ^i​(λj)=(t+1)​pi​(λj)​(L~i−ℓ^t+1​(λj))\widehat{\psi}_{i}(\lambda_{j})=(t+1)p_{i}(\lambda_{j})\bigl(\widetilde{L}_{i}-\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})\bigr) to approximate the first-order linear expansion of the error. Lemma F.11 shows that the implementation approximates the true first-order error contributions in average squared error. We show empirically that the average squared discrepancy between the implemented and ideal scores decreases to zero on a large dataset in Appendix G.6.4. This lemma connects the theoretical first-order expansion with our implementation.

Proof Sketch: The implementation and the theoretical first-order term differ in weight and in the base risk estimate. For the weight, the implementation uses the Sinkhorn weight, while the theoretical first-order term uses the importance weight with the "average" logging policy. We first show that the error is negligible as tt increases. For the base risk estimate, where the theoretical first-order term uses the true risk while the implementation uses the estimated risk, we show that the risk estimation error is also negligible. Combining these two terms, we show that the averaging error between ψ^i\widehat{\psi}_{i} and ψi\psi_{i} vanishes.

Proof.

Fix a candidate λj\lambda_{j} and abbreviate

q=qj,ℓ=ℓt+1​(λj),ℓ^=ℓ^t+1​(λj),wi=q⁡(Ai∣Xi)b⁡(Ai∣Xi).q=q_{j},\qquad\ell=\ell_{t+1}(\lambda_{j}),\qquad\widehat{\ell}=\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda_{j}),\qquad w_{i}=\frac{q(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{b(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}.

All constants below are independent of tt.

pi=ω~i∑k=1t+1ω~k,ω~i=ωi1+c​ωi,ωi=q⁡(Ai∣Xi)beff​(Ai∣Xi),p_{i}=\frac{\widetilde{\omega}_{i}}{\sum_{k=1}^{t+1}\widetilde{\omega}_{k}},\qquad\widetilde{\omega}_{i}=\frac{\omega_{i}}{1+c\omega_{i}},\qquad\omega_{i}=\frac{q(A_{i}\mid X_{i})}{b_{\mathrm{eff}}(A_{i}\mid X_{i})},

where

beff=b⁡(1+β𝖳​f),‖β‖≤C​Δt,0<c≤C/t.b_{\mathrm{eff}}=b(1+\beta^{\mathsf{T}}f),\qquad\|\beta\|\leq C\sqrt{\Delta_{t}},\qquad 0<c\leq C/t.

Uniform positivity and boundedness of ff imply

maxi≤t+1⁡|ωi−wi|≤C​Δt,maxi≤t+1⁡|ω~i−ωi|≤C/t.\max_{i\leq t+1}|\omega_{i}-w_{i}|\leq C\sqrt{\Delta_{t}},\qquad\max_{i\leq t+1}|\widetilde{\omega}_{i}-\omega_{i}|\leq C/t.

Consequently,

maxi≤t+1⁡|ω~i−wi|≤C⁡(Δt+t−1).\max_{i\leq t+1}|\widetilde{\omega}_{i}-w_{i}|\leq C(\sqrt{\Delta_{t}}+t^{-1}). (F.7)

The quantities wiw_{i} and ω~i\widetilde{\omega}_{i} are uniformly bounded above and away from zero.

For the real observations, define

Mt:=1t​∑i=1t{wi−𝔼⁡[wi∣ℱi−1]}.M_{t}:=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\bigl\{w_{i}-\mathbb{E}[w_{i}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]\bigr\}.

𝔼​Mt2≤C/t.\mathbb{E}M_{t}^{2}\leq C/t.

𝔼⁡[wi∣ℱi−1]=𝔼b​[(1+θi𝖳​f)​w]=1+θi𝖳​𝔼b​[f​w].\mathbb{E}[w_{i}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=\mathbb{E}_{b}[(1+\theta_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}f)w]=1+\theta_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbb{E}_{b}[fw].

Therefore, with θ¯=t−1​∑i=1tθi\bar{\theta}=t^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\theta_{i},

1t​∑i=1twi=1+θ¯𝖳​𝔼b​[f​w]+Mt,‖θ¯‖≤Δt.\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_{i}=1+\bar{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbb{E}_{b}[fw]+M_{t},\qquad\|\bar{\theta}\|\leq\sqrt{\Delta_{t}}.

Let

W¯t:=1t+1​∑i=1t+1ω~i.\overline{W}_{t}:=\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t+1}\widetilde{\omega}_{i}.

Using (F.7), the preceding identity, and the boundedness of the test-point weight gives

|W¯t−1|≤C⁡(Δt+|Mt|+t−1).|\overline{W}_{t}-1|\leq C(\sqrt{\Delta_{t}}+|M_{t}|+t^{-1}).

Moreover, W¯t\overline{W}_{t} is bounded away from zero. Since

(t+1)​pi=ω~iW¯t,(t+1)p_{i}=\frac{\widetilde{\omega}_{i}}{\overline{W}_{t}},

we obtain

maxi≤t+1⁡|(t+1)​pi−wi|≤C⁡(Δt+|Mt|+t−1).\max_{i\leq t+1}|(t+1)p_{i}-w_{i}|\leq C(\sqrt{\Delta_{t}}+|M_{t}|+t^{-1}).

In particular,

𝔼⁡[maxi≤t+1⁡|(t+1)​pi−wi|2]≤C⁡(Δt+t−1),maxi≤t+1⁡(t+1)​pi≤C.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{i\leq t+1}|(t+1)p_{i}-w_{i}|^{2}\right]\leq C(\Delta_{t}+t^{-1}),\qquad\max_{i\leq t+1}(t+1)p_{i}\leq C. (F.8)

Lemma F.7 gives

ℓ^−ℓ=1t+1​∑i=1tψi​(λj)+rt+1​(λj).\widehat{\ell}-\ell=\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})+r_{t+1}(\lambda_{j}).

𝔼⁡[(∑i=1tψi​(λj))2]≤C​t.\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{t}\psi_{i}(\lambda_{j})\right)^{2}\right]\leq Ct.

The first term is controlled by (F.8), the second by (F.9), and the third satisfies

1t​∑i=1tdi,j2≤C​1t​∑i=1t‖θi‖2≤C​Δt.\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}d_{i,j}^{2}\leq C\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\|\theta_{i}\|^{2}\leq C\Delta_{t}.

𝔼⁡[et+1 2]≤C⁡(Δt+t−1)⟶0.\mathbb{E}[e_{t+1}^{\,2}]\leq C(\Delta_{t}+t^{-1})\longrightarrow 0.

F.1 Proof of Theorem 4.5

We prove Theorem 4.5 by combining the three lemmas. Lemma F.7 writes the true estimation error as an average of mean-zero contributions plus a negligible remainder. Together with the covariance stabilization in Lemma F.9, we then show that the estimation error of each candidate policy induces a Gaussian limit. Lemma F.11 then ensures that the bootstrap score construction recovers the same limiting covariance, demonstrating the effectiveness of the bootstrap score in approximating the estimation error. Finally, as the distribution of the bootstrap estimation matches the true error distribution, the maximum-error distribution matches, yielding consistent bootstrap quantiles.

Proof of Theorem 4.5.

Throughout the proof, vectors collect the coordinates indexed by λ1,…,λK\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{K}. Write

ℓt+1=(ℓt+1​(λj))j=1K,ℓ^t+1=(ℓ^t+1​(λj))j=1K.\bm{\ell}_{t+1}=\bigl(\ell_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})\bigr)_{j=1}^{K},\qquad\widehat{\bm{\ell}}_{t+1}=\bigl(\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda_{j})\bigr)_{j=1}^{K}.
Step 1: the true error has a Gaussian limit.

By Lemma F.7,

t+1​(ℓ^t+1−ℓt+1)=St+t+1​rt+1,St:=1t+1​∑i=1tψi,\sqrt{t+1}\,\bigl(\widehat{\bm{\ell}}_{t+1}-\bm{\ell}_{t+1}\bigr)=S_{t}+\sqrt{t+1}\,r_{t+1},\qquad S_{t}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t+1}}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\psi_{i},

where

𝔼​‖t+1​rt+1‖2⟶0.\mathbb{E}\|\sqrt{t+1}\,r_{t+1}\|^{2}\longrightarrow 0.

The vectors ψi\psi_{i} are uniformly bounded martingale differences. In particular, for every η>0\eta>0,

1t+1∑i=1t𝔼[∥ψi∥2𝟏{∥ψi∥>ηt+1}|ℱi−1]=0\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\psi_{i}\|^{2}\mathbf{1}\{\|\psi_{i}\|>\eta\sqrt{t+1}\}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{i-1}\right]=0

for all sufficiently large tt. Thus the conditional Lindeberg condition holds.

Lemma F.9 gives

Vt+1:=1t+1​∑i=1t𝔼⁡[ψi​ψi𝖳∣ℱi−1]→𝑝V.V_{t+1}:=\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]\xrightarrow{p}V.

The martingale central limit theorem therefore yields

St⇒Z,Z∼N⁡(0,V).S_{t}\Rightarrow Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,V).

The remainder converges to zero in probability after scaling by t+1\sqrt{t+1}. Since −Z-Z has the same distribution as ZZ,

t+1​(ℓt+1−ℓ^t+1)⇒N⁡(0,V).\sqrt{t+1}\,\bigl(\bm{\ell}_{t+1}-\widehat{\bm{\ell}}_{t+1}\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,V). (F.10)

The L2L^{2} remainder also implies convergence of the actual error covariance. Indeed, martingale orthogonality gives

𝔼​St=0,𝔼⁡[St​St𝖳]=𝔼​Vt+1⟶V,\mathbb{E}S_{t}=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[S_{t}S_{t}^{\mathsf{T}}]=\mathbb{E}V_{t+1}\longrightarrow V,

where convergence of expectations follows from uniform boundedness of Vt+1V_{t+1}. The remainder covariance and its cross terms with StS_{t} vanish by Cauchy–Schwarz. Consequently,

(t+1)​Cov⁡(ℓt+1−ℓ^t+1)⟶V.(t+1)\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(\bm{\ell}_{t+1}-\widehat{\bm{\ell}}_{t+1}\bigr)\longrightarrow V. (F.11)
Step 2: the bootstrap estimates the same covariance.

Define

V~t+1:=1t+1​∑i=1tψi​ψi𝖳.\widetilde{V}_{t+1}:=\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t}\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}.

Each entry of

ψi​ψi𝖳−𝔼⁡[ψi​ψi𝖳∣ℱi−1]\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}-\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]

is a bounded martingale difference. Since KK is fixed, martingale orthogonality gives

𝔼​‖V~t+1−Vt+1‖F2≤C/t.\mathbb{E}\|\widetilde{V}_{t+1}-V_{t+1}\|_{F}^{2}\leq C/t.

Together with Lemma F.9, this implies

V~t+1→𝑝V.\widetilde{V}_{t+1}\xrightarrow{p}V.

Now define the covariance estimate from the actual bootstrap scores:

V^t+1:=1t+1​∑i=1t+1ψ^i​ψ^i𝖳=(t+1)​∑i=1t+1ϕ^i​ϕ^i𝖳,\widehat{V}_{t+1}:=\frac{1}{t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{t+1}\widehat{\psi}_{i}\widehat{\psi}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}=(t+1)\sum_{i=1}^{t+1}\widehat{\phi}_{i}\widehat{\phi}_{i}^{\mathsf{T}},

where ψ^i=(t+1)​ϕ^i\widehat{\psi}_{i}=(t+1)\widehat{\phi}_{i}. Let et+1e_{t+1} be the square root of the discrepancy defined in Lemma F.11. Expanding the outer products and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields

‖V^t+1−V~t+1‖≤2​C​et+1+et+1 2→𝑝0.\|\widehat{V}_{t+1}-\widetilde{V}_{t+1}\|\leq 2Ce_{t+1}+e_{t+1}^{\,2}\xrightarrow{p}0.

The test-point term is included in et+1 2e_{t+1}^{\,2} through its zero ideal contribution. It follows that

V^t+1→𝑝V.\widehat{V}_{t+1}\xrightarrow{p}V. (F.12)

Conditional on 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}, the scores are fixed and the multipliers are independent standard Gaussian variables. Hence the bootstrap vector satisfies the exact conditional identity

t+1​𝑮^t+1∗|𝒟t∼N⁡(0,V^t+1),\sqrt{t+1}\,\widehat{\bm{G}}_{t+1}^{*}\mid\mathcal{D}_{t}\sim N(0,\widehat{V}_{t+1}), (F.13)

where

𝑮^t+1∗:=(G^t+1∗​(λ1),…,G^t+1∗​(λK))𝖳.\widehat{\bm{G}}_{t+1}^{*}:=\bigl(\widehat{G}_{t+1}^{*}(\lambda_{1}),\ldots,\widehat{G}_{t+1}^{*}(\lambda_{K})\bigr)^{\mathsf{T}}.

Step 3: the distributions of the maxima are close.

Let

W:=maxj≤K⁡Zj,Z∼N⁡(0,V),F⁡(x):=ℙ⁡(W≤x).W:=\max_{j\leq K}Z_{j},\qquad Z\sim N(0,V),\qquad F(x):=\mathbb{P}(W\leq x).

By Lemma F.9, Vj​j>0V_{jj}>0 for every jj, so each ZjZ_{j} has a continuous distribution. For every x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R},

ℙ⁡(W=x)≤∑j=1Kℙ⁡(Zj=x)=0.\mathbb{P}(W=x)\leq\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbb{P}(Z_{j}=x)=0.

The maximum is a continuous function. Applying the continuous mapping theorem to (F.10) gives

t+1​Tt+1⇒W.\sqrt{t+1}\,T_{t+1}\Rightarrow W.

Because the limiting distribution function is continuous, this convergence is uniform at the level of distribution functions:

supx∈ℝ|ℙ⁡(t+1​Tt+1≤x)−F⁡(x)|⟶0.\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{t+1}\,T_{t+1}\leq x)-F(x)\right|\longrightarrow 0. (F.14)

To handle the conditional bootstrap distribution, take U∼N⁡(0,IK)U\sim N(0,I_{K}) independently of 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} and couple the two Gaussian vectors as

V^t+11/2​UandV1/2​U.\widehat{V}_{t+1}^{1/2}U\quad\text{and}\quad V^{1/2}U.

The positive semidefinite square-root map is continuous, including at singular matrices. Therefore,

‖V^t+11/2−V1/2‖F→𝑝0.\|\widehat{V}_{t+1}^{1/2}-V^{1/2}\|_{F}\xrightarrow{p}0.

Using

|maxj⁡xj−maxj⁡yj|≤‖x−y‖2|\max_{j}x_{j}-\max_{j}y_{j}|\leq\|x-y\|_{2}

and conditional Markov’s inequality, for any η>0\eta>0,

ℙ⁡(|W^t−W0|>η∣𝒟t)≤‖V^t+11/2−V1/2‖F2η2.\mathbb{P}(|\widehat{W}_{t}-W_{0}|>\eta\mid\mathcal{D}_{t})\leq\frac{\|\widehat{V}_{t+1}^{1/2}-V^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}}{\eta^{2}}.

A distribution-function sandwich then gives

supx|ℙ⁡(t+1​Tt+1∗≤x∣𝒟t)−F⁡(x)|\displaystyle\sup_{x}\left|\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{t+1}\,T_{t+1}^{*}\leq x\mid\mathcal{D}_{t})-F(x)\right|
≤‖V^t+11/2−V1/2‖F2η2+supx{F⁡(x+η)−F⁡(x−η)}.\displaystyle\qquad\leq\frac{\|\widehat{V}_{t+1}^{1/2}-V^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}}{\eta^{2}}+\sup_{x}\{F(x+\eta)-F(x-\eta)\}.

For fixed η\eta, the first term converges to zero in probability as t→∞t\to\infty. The second tends to zero as η↓0\eta\downarrow 0, because a continuous distribution function is uniformly continuous. Consequently,

supx|ℙ⁡(t+1​Tt+1∗≤x∣𝒟t)−F⁡(x)|→𝑝0.\sup_{x}\left|\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{t+1}\,T_{t+1}^{*}\leq x\mid\mathcal{D}_{t})-F(x)\right|\xrightarrow{p}0. (F.15)

Combining (F.14) and (F.15) by the triangle inequality, and changing variables x=t+1​ux=\sqrt{t+1}\,u, proves

supu∈ℝ|ℙ⁡(Tt+1≤u)−ℙ⁡(Tt+1∗≤u∣𝒟t)|→𝑝0.\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}}\left|\mathbb{P}(T_{t+1}\leq u)-\mathbb{P}(T_{t+1}^{*}\leq u\mid\mathcal{D}_{t})\right|\xrightarrow{p}0.
Step 4: quantile consistency gives simultaneous coverage.

We first verify that the limiting quantile is unique. The Gaussian vector ZZ has positive density relative to its support subspace

S=range⁡(V1/2).S=\operatorname{range}(V^{1/2}).

The image of SS under z↦maxj⁡zjz\mapsto\max_{j}z_{j} is either ℝ\mathbb{R} or [0,∞)[0,\infty): a positive value exists, positive scaling gives every positive value, and if a negative value exists, scaling also gives every negative value. Every open interval intersecting the interior of this image has a nonempty relatively open preimage in SS, and therefore positive Gaussian probability. Thus FF is strictly increasing on the interior of its support.

For fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), let

c:=F−1​(1−δ).c:=F^{-1}(1-\delta).

Continuity and strict increase imply

F⁡(c)=1−δ,F⁡(c−η)<1−δ⁡<F⁡(c+η)for every ​η>​0.F(c)=1-\delta,\qquad F(c-\eta)<1-\delta<F(c+\eta)\quad\text{for every }\eta>0.

Qt:=t+1​q1−δ,t+1∗.Q_{t}:=\sqrt{t+1}\,q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*}.

Uniform conditional distribution-function convergence in (F.15) implies

Qt→𝑝c.Q_{t}\xrightarrow{p}c.

Indeed, with probability tending to one, the conditional bootstrap distribution function is below 1−δ1-\delta at c−ηc-\eta and above 1−δ1-\delta at c+ηc+\eta, placing its quantile between these points.

The critical value and the true error may depend on the same data. To obtain coverage without an independence assumption, use the inequalities

ℙ⁡(t+1​Tt+1≤c−η)−ℙ⁡(|Qt−c|>η)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{t+1}\,T_{t+1}\leq c-\eta)-\mathbb{P}(|Q_{t}-c|>\eta)
≤ℙ⁡(Tt+1≤q1−δ,t+1∗)\displaystyle\qquad\leq\mathbb{P}(T_{t+1}\leq q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*})
≤ℙ⁡(t+1​Tt+1≤c+η)+ℙ⁡(|Qt−c|>η).\displaystyle\qquad\leq\mathbb{P}(\sqrt{t+1}\,T_{t+1}\leq c+\eta)+\mathbb{P}(|Q_{t}-c|>\eta).

Finally, by the definition of Tt+1T_{t+1},

{Tt+1≤q1−δ,t+1∗}={ℓt+1(λ)≤ℓ^t+1(λ)+q1−δ,t+1∗ for all λ∈Λt+1}.\{T_{t+1}\leq q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*}\}=\left\{\ell_{t+1}(\lambda)\leq\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*}\text{ for all }\lambda\in\Lambda_{t+1}\right\}.

Now we prove the asymptotic high-probability risk control in Corollary 4.7.

Proof.

Let q1−δ,t+1∗q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*} be the conditional (1−δ)(1-\delta)-quantile of Tt+1∗T_{t+1}^{*}:

q1−δ,t+1∗:=inf{q∈ℝ:ℙ(Tt+1∗≤q∣Z1:t+1)≥1−δ}.q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*}:=\inf\left\{q\in\mathbb{R}:\mathbb{P}(T_{t+1}^{*}\leq q\mid Z_{1:t+1})\geq 1-\delta\right\}.

By the bootstrap consistency above and the continuity of the limiting Gaussian maximum at the (1−δ)(1-\delta)-quantile,

ℙ⁡(Tt+1≤q1−δ,t+1∗)→1−δ.\mathbb{P}(T_{t+1}\leq q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*})\to 1-\delta.

By definition of Tt+1T_{t+1}, the event

Tt+1≤q1−δ,t+1∗T_{t+1}\leq q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*}

is equivalent to

maxλ∈Λt+1⁡(ℓt+1​(λ)−ℓ^t+1​(λ))≤q1−δ,t+1∗.\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{t+1}}\bigl(\ell_{t+1}(\lambda)-\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda)\bigr)\leq q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*}.

Equivalently,

ℓt+1​(λ)≤ℓ^t+1​(λ)+q1−δ,t+1∗,∀λ∈Λt+1.\ell_{t+1}(\lambda)\leq\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*},\qquad\forall\lambda\in\Lambda_{t+1}.

Therefore,

ℙ⁡(ℓt+1​(λ)≤ℓ^t+1​(λ)+q1−δ,t+1∗​for all ​λ∈Λt+1)→1−δ.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\ell_{t+1}(\lambda)\leq\widehat{\ell}_{t+1}(\lambda)+q_{1-\delta,t+1}^{*}\ \text{for all }\lambda\in\Lambda_{t+1}\right)\to 1-\delta.

This completes the proof. ∎

Appendix G Experiment Details and Additional Experiments

G.1 Datasets and Experimental Setup

G.1.1 Breast cancer diagnosis.

We convert the breast cancer classification dataset into a binary contextual bandit problem following [38, 39]. Each feature vector is treated as a context xx, and the action space is 𝒜={0,1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\}, where a=1a=1 denotes predicting malignant and a=0a=0 denotes predicting benign. The reward is the classification accuracy reward r(x,a,y)=𝟏{a=y}r(x,a,y)=\mathbf{1}\{a=y\}. The risk of interest is the false-negative rate R⁡(π)=Prπ⁡(a=0∣y=1)R(\pi)=\Pr_{\pi}(a=0\mid y=1), and the goal is to select a policy at each round satisfying

R⁡(π)≤α.R(\pi)\leq\alpha.

The base policy is a neural network classifier with logits fθ​(x)∈ℝ2f_{\theta}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. The control parameter is a positive-class bias λ=b\lambda=b, and the controlled policy is

πθ,λ​(a∣x)=softmax​(fθ​(x)+[0λ])a.\pi_{\theta,\lambda}(a\mid x)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(f_{\theta}(x)+\begin{bmatrix}0\\ \lambda\end{bmatrix}\right)_{a}.

Larger bb makes the policy more likely to select the positive class, thereby reducing false negatives but potentially increasing false positives. The πθ=softmax⁡(fθ​(x))\pi_{\theta}=\mathrm{softmax}(f_{\theta}(x)) is optimized every round with importance weights. Here, the FNR risk function is monotonic in λ\lambda. We then train the policy with a policy gradient using self-normalized importance sampling. We use accuracy as the reward.

G.1.2 Stock investment.

We also evaluate on a six-action stock investment bandit. Each context xx contains market features, and each action a∈{1,…,6}a\in\{1,\ldots,6\} corresponds to selecting one asset. The realized reward is the normalized profit of the selected asset. The risk is the probability of selecting the worst-performing action,

L⁡(π)=Prπ⁡(a=arg⁡mina′∈𝒜⁡r⁡(x,a′)).L(\pi)=\Pr_{\pi}\!\left(a=\arg\min_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}r(x,a^{\prime})\right).

The goal is to select a policy whose worst-action selection risk is below a target level α\alpha.

The policy is parameterized by a neural network: πθ,λ​(a|x)=softmax⁡(r^θ​(x,a)−λ​l^​(x,a))\pi_{\theta,\lambda}(a|x)=\mathrm{softmax}(\hat{r}_{\theta}(x,a)-\lambda\hat{l}(x,a)), where r^\hat{r} and l^\hat{l} are the estimated reward and risk functions respectively. They are trained with MSE loss. The control parameter λ\lambda adjusts the policy’s decision rule over candidate actions, producing a candidate family {πλ:λ∈Λ}\{\pi_{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda\}. Unlike the breast cancer task, the induced risk curve over λ\lambda can be non-monotone. Therefore, in addition to comparing different risk evaluators, we use this task to test the proposed Gaussian multiplier bootstrap correction. The bootstrap estimates the maximum risk-estimation error over Λ\Lambda and adds a uniform inflation term to all candidate risk estimates before selection.

G.1.3 Safe Question Answering with SafetyBench.

We evaluate our method on SafetyBench, a benchmark containing 11,435 multiple-choice questions covering seven categories of safety concerns. We use its English version and formulate the task as selective single-answer question answering: the system either returns one answer option or abstains. Our objective is to answer as many questions correctly as possible while keeping the error rate among answered questions below a target level α\alpha. We use Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as the base language model.

Gate. For each checkpoint tt, we independently train a gate gt​(x,a)∈[0,1]g_{t}(x,a)\in[0,1] to predict whether a proposed answer aa to question xx is correct. The gate is an ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized logistic classifier with 47 input features: 15 features describing model confidence, answer-choice statistics, and text lengths, together with 16 principal components of the prompt representation and 16 principal components of the prompt-with-answer representation. All representations are extracted from the current checkpoint. The PCA transformations, feature standardization, and classifier are fitted separately at each checkpoint using 2,000 gate-training questions. For each question, one answer is sampled from the current model, and its correctness provides the supervision. A separate set of 512 development questions defines 41 candidate thresholds: 39 gate-score quantiles and the two endpoints −∞-\infty and +∞+\infty. Development labels are not used to select these thresholds.

Policy. Let 𝒜⁡(x)\mathcal{A}(x) denote the valid answer options for question xx. The model induces an answer distribution

qt​(a∣x)=exp⁡{zt​(x,a)/Ttemp}∑a′∈𝒜⁡(x)exp⁡{zt​(x,a′)/Ttemp},Ttemp=0.8,q_{t}(a\mid x)=\frac{\exp\{z_{t}(x,a)/T_{\mathrm{temp}}\}}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}(x)}\exp\{z_{t}(x,a^{\prime})/T_{\mathrm{temp}}\}},\qquad T_{\mathrm{temp}}=0.8,

where zt​(x,a)z_{t}(x,a) is the logit of the corresponding answer-option token. Given a threshold β\beta, we first sample a proposed answer from qt(⋅∣x)q_{t}(\cdot\mid x) and return it only when gt​(x,a)≥βg_{t}(x,a)\geq\beta. Otherwise, the system abstains. Thus, the controlled policy is

πt,β(a∣x)=qt(a∣x)𝟏{gt(x,a)≥β},a∈𝒜(x),\pi_{t,\beta}(a\mid x)=q_{t}(a\mid x)\mathbf{1}\{g_{t}(x,a)\geq\beta\},\qquad a\in\mathcal{A}(x),
πt,β(⊥∣x)=1−∑a∈𝒜⁡(x)πt,β(a∣x),\pi_{t,\beta}(\bot\mid x)=1-\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}(x)}\pi_{t,\beta}(a\mid x),

where ⊥\bot denotes abstention. The control method selects β\beta at each round.

Policy sequence. After removing duplicate or ambiguously labeled records, we retain 11,409 questions and construct internal splits of 4,409 training questions, 1,000 validation questions, and 6,000 questions reserved for gate fitting and risk-control evaluation. We fine-tune the base model using LoRA with rank 64 and scaling parameter 128 on the attention and MLP projections. Training uses supervised cross-entropy over valid answer options, an effective batch size of 32, and AdamW with a peak learning rate of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} followed by cosine decay. Five training epochs produce 690 optimizer updates. We save a checkpoint every 69 updates, obtaining eleven models at steps 0,69,…,6900,69,\ldots,690, including the initial model. These checkpoints, paired with their respective gates, define the sequence of candidate policy families. The experiment replays this fixed training trajectory: Calibration feedback does not update the language model. Figure 4 reports each checkpoint’s accuracy during full-data fine-tuning. We then use each checkpoint as the policy for online calibration.

Metrics. For calibration repetition bb and checkpoint tt, let Cb​tC_{bt} denote the probability of answering and Eb​tE_{bt} the probability of answering incorrectly under the selected policy. Its conditional risk is Rb​t=Eb​t/Cb​tR_{bt}=E_{bt}/C_{bt} when Cb​t>0C_{bt}>0. Across B=200B=200 repetitions, we report the mean refusal rate and pooled conditional risk:

Refusalt=1−1B​∑b=1BCb​t,Riskt=∑b=1BEb​t∑b=1BCb​t.\mathrm{Refusal}_{t}=1-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}C_{bt},\qquad\mathrm{Risk}_{t}=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}E_{bt}}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}C_{bt}}.

We also report cumulative expected wrong answers,

CumWrongt=MB​∑b=1B∑s=0tEb​s,M=2464.\mathrm{CumWrong}_{t}=\frac{M}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{s=0}^{t}E_{bs},\qquad M=2464.

and the risk satisfaction rate,

Satisfactiont=1B∑b=1B𝟏{Eb​t≤αCb​t}.\mathrm{Satisfaction}_{t}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf{1}\{E_{bt}\leq\alpha C_{bt}\}.

A policy that always abstains has undefined conditional risk; it is counted as nonviolating in the satisfaction rate, and its occurrence is reported separately. Cumulative reward includes all evaluated checkpoints up to tt and excludes the calibration warmup.

Procedure. The 6,000 reserved questions are partitioned into 2,000 gate-training questions, 512 gate-development questions, a calibration pool of 2,464 questions, and a separate audit pool of 1,024 questions. Each calibration trajectory starts with m0=512m_{0}=512 labeled observations sampled with replacement from the calibration pool using the initial answer policy q0q_{0}. At checkpoint tt, the current gate rescores all historical question–answer pairs while preserving their original answers, error labels, and logging probabilities. The applicable controllers also receive an unlabeled probe sampled from qtq_{t}. After threshold selection, the probe label is revealed, and the record is appended together with 128 additional labeled observations from qtq_{t}. Consequently, the history available at checkpoint tt contains m0+129​tm_{0}+129t records. These observations are collected from the base answer policy, irrespective of the selected abstention threshold.

We set α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and use 2,000 Gaussian multiplier bootstrap draws with δ=0.2\delta=0.2 for the high-probability variant, corresponding to a nominal confidence level of 1−δ=0.81-\delta=0.8. The methods share calibration histories and candidate threshold grids within each repetition. We also include a historical LTT–Bonferroni baseline, which tests the 40 nontrivial candidates using one-sided exact binomial bounds at level δ/40\delta/40. This baseline ignores policy shift; its usual i.i.d. guarantee is not assumed to hold for histories generated by changing policies.

We perform 200 calibration repetitions with the model checkpoints and gates held fixed. After recording the threshold selections, we compute the main metrics by exactly integrating over all valid answer options and the uniform distribution on the 2,464 question calibration pool. Thus, the main evaluation concerns this fixed finite reference distribution; the separate audit pool provides a secondary evaluation. Risk satisfaction is measured separately at each checkpoint and does not imply a simultaneous guarantee over the entire trajectory.

G.1.4 Factual Medical Question Answering

We use the MedLFQA dataset. Each record contains a medical question, a generated response, atomic claims extracted from the response, and binary labels indicating whether the reference answer supports each claim. Following the original preprocessing, we obtain 4,805 records containing 81,196 atomic claims and use the cached log-probability scores for claim filtering. We repeat the experiment over 1,000 random record-level splits, each containing 3,363 calibration records and 1,442 held-out test records. Original records, including repeated question texts, are retained.

Control: The policy is a threshold-based filter: a claim is retained if its score is at least λ\lambda. For each response, the loss is the false discovery proportion (FDP), defined as the fraction of retained claims that are unsupported, with loss zero when no claims are retained. Risk is the expected response-level FDP, while utility is the recall of supported claims. This is a static post-processing task without feedback-induced covariate shift, so all importance weights equal one. For each split, we construct approximately 200 candidate thresholds from the calibration scores using the original implementation. Our method uses Gaussian bootstrap calibration with nominal failure probability δ=0.2\delta=0.2 and 2,000 joint Gaussian draws to estimate a simultaneous risk upper bound over the candidates. We select the smallest threshold whose upper bound does not exceed α\alpha, with an all-reject policy as a fallback. We report mean held-out FDP, supported-claim recall, and held-out risk satisfaction rate, defined as the fraction of splits for which the mean test FDP is at most α\alpha.

Baselines. We compare against gCRC, Monotonized CRC, and Learn Then Test (LTT). gCRC scans thresholds from high to low and returns the preceding threshold when the CRC-corrected empirical risk first exceeds α\alpha. Monotonized CRC first replaces each response’s loss by L~i​(λ)=maxλ′≥λ⁡Li​(λ′)\widetilde{L}_{i}(\lambda)=\max_{\lambda^{\prime}\geq\lambda}L_{i}(\lambda^{\prime}) over the candidate grid, then applies standard CRC to these losses. Both CRC methods use the correction (∑i=1nLi+1)/(n+1)(\sum_{i=1}^{n}L_{i}+1)/(n+1), with the appropriate original or monotonized losses. LTT follows the original implementation’s fixed-sequence Hoeffding–Bentkus tests, using δLTT=δ\delta_{\mathrm{LTT}}=\delta. All methods select thresholds using calibration data and are evaluated using the original, unmodified FDP on held-out records.

Summary: Table 1 summarizes the control parameters, their effects on the distribution, and the risk metrics.

G.2 Distribution Shift Type and Control Problem

Risk Control vs. Policy Control Our primary setting controls deployment risk through policy calibration: the parameter λ\lambda modifies the action distribution of πλ\pi_{\lambda}, thereby changing its expected deployment risk or the expected risk of the collected data. Policy control is thus both a mechanism for achieving risk control and a specific problem within the broader risk control framework. In the standard conformal risk control formulation [4], different from "policy" control, λ\lambda instead parameterizes a prediction rule (e.g., classification threshold) and its associated risk LλL_{\lambda}. Although primarily motivated by policy control, our framework accommodates both policy-based and risk-based risk control. In settings without distribution shift, our high-probability control procedure can also be applied to standard risk estimators for high-probability guarantees. When distribution shift exists, our risk estimator can be applied to risk-based risk control alongside the high-probability control method, provided the shift can be quantified for reweighting. This includes both changes in the action distribution induced by policy updates and changes in the covariate distribution, as in the covariate-shift case in CRC. Our experiments include both policy calibration and direct calibration of parameterized loss functions.

Feedback Covariate Shift vs. Non-Adaptive Covariate Shift Our method is primarily motivated by feedback covariate shift, where policies learned from past observations affect subsequent future data collection, inducing dependence across data observations. However, the permutation-weighting method is also applicable to covariate shift without feedback, including changes in the covariate distribution or data collected under multiple non-adaptive policies, and performs well compared with baselines. Such settings do not require the history-dependent policy updates that characterize feedback covariate shift. Our framework therefore accommodates both feedback and non-adaptive covariate shift, provided that the relevant sampling distributions can be characterized to construct the weights.

G.3 Baselines

Online CRC (O-CRC)

Online CRC extends conformal risk control under distribution shift to the online policy-learning setting. At each round, it evaluates each candidate policy using a sample-wise importance-weighted risk estimate, where the weight corrects the mismatch between the candidate policy and the historical data-collection policy. It then selects a candidate whose estimated risk is below the target threshold. This baseline corresponds to using local importance weights without the proposed permutation-based correction for feedback covariate shift.

RollingRC

RollingRC extends adaptive conformal inference to general online risk control by sequentially updating a calibration parameter according to the observed risk loss. Specifically, after observing the realized loss at each round, it updates the calibration parameter in the direction that would reduce future deviations from the target risk level.

Conformal Policy Control (CPC)

CPC uses a policy-control rule that orders candidate policies from safest to most aggressive and selects the most aggressive candidate whose conservatively adjusted weighted empirical risk remains below the target threshold. In our experiments, we use only this policy-selection rule as a baseline, without the safe-policy interpolation mechanism.

Learn-then-Test (LTT)

Learn-then-Test treats each candidate policy as a hypothesis and tests whether its risk is below the target threshold. It selects policies that pass a finite-sample risk test, typically using a multiple-testing correction to account for searching over many candidates. While LTT can provide high-probability guarantees under its assumptions, it is often conservative and designed for i.i.d. data.

Upper Confidence Bound Risk Control (UCB-RC).

For each candidate λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, we compute a weighted empirical risk estimate

ℓ^t​(λ)=∑i=1twi​(λ)​Li,∑i=1twi​(λ)=1.\widehat{\ell}_{t}(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_{i}(\lambda)L_{i},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_{i}(\lambda)=1.

Assuming Li∈[0,1]L_{i}\in[0,1], we construct a Hoeffding-style upper confidence bound

UCBt​(λ)=ℓ^t​(λ)+log⁡(|Λ|/δ)2​neff​(λ),neff​(λ)=1∑i=1twi​(λ)2.\mathrm{UCB}_{t}(\lambda)=\widehat{\ell}_{t}(\lambda)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(|\Lambda|/\delta)}{2\,n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)}},\qquad n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_{i}(\lambda)^{2}}.

The selected policy is restricted to the feasible set

Λ^UCB={λ∈Λ:UCBt​(λ)≤α}.\widehat{\Lambda}_{\mathrm{UCB}}=\left\{\lambda\in\Lambda:\mathrm{UCB}_{t}(\lambda)\leq\alpha\right\}.

We can then select the λ\lambda with the highest estimated reward.

Multi-step permutation weight

Prinster et al. [6] approximate the exact permutation weight by keeping only the dynamic factors from the most recent dd rounds. For each candidate point ZiZ_{i}, its dd-step weight is defined as the normalized total likelihood of all permutations that place ZiZ_{i} at the target position t+1t+1:

pt+1(d)​(Zi∣Ez(t))\displaystyle p^{(d)}_{t+1}(Z_{i}\mid E_{z}^{(t)}) =∑σ:σ⁡(n+t)=i∏j=t+1−dt+1p(Zσ⁡(j)∣Zσ⁡(1),…,Zσ⁡(j−1))∑σ∏j=t+1−dt+1p⁡(Zσ⁡(j)∣Zσ⁡(1),…,Zσ⁡(j−1))\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(n+t)=i}\prod_{j=t+1-d}^{t+1}p\!\left(Z_{\sigma(j)}\mid Z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,Z_{\sigma(j-1)}\right)}{\sum_{\sigma}\prod_{j=t+1-d}^{t+1}p\!\left(Z_{\sigma(j)}\mid Z_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,Z_{\sigma(j-1)}\right)}
=∑σ:σ⁡(n+t)=i∏j=t+1−dt+1πθ,λj(Zσ⁡(j)∣Xσ⁡(j))∑σ∏j=t+1−dt+1πθ,λj​(Zσ⁡(j)∣Xσ⁡(j))\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\sigma:\,\sigma(n+t)=i}\prod_{j=t+1-d}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{j}\!\left(Z_{\sigma(j)}\mid X_{\sigma(j)}\right)}{\sum_{\sigma}\prod_{j=t+1-d}^{t+1}\pi_{\theta,\lambda}^{j}\!\left(Z_{\sigma(j)}\mid X_{\sigma(j)}\right)}

Here, the numerator sums the truncated likelihood over all orderings in which ziz_{i} is assigned to the final target timestep, while the denominator normalizes over all possible orderings. Thus, pt+1(d)​(zi∣Ez(t))p^{(d)}_{t+1}(z_{i}\mid E_{z}^{(t)}) forms a probability distribution over the observed points.

G.4 Reward of the risk control experiments

In Figure 5, we show our method’s reward compared with the baselines. We see that in Stock Investment, we receives a similar reward with lower risk. In the other two cases, our method receives a lower reward than the baselines because we satisfy the risk constraint.

G.5 High-Probability Risk Control: Conservatism and Robustness to Distribution Shift

Section 5.2 compares RCL-HP with several high-probability risk-control methods, including LTT. Here, we further analyze two aspects of high-probability risk control: conservatism across nominal confidence levels and robustness to distribution shift. We compare RCL-HP with LTT and UCB-RC, where UCB-RC applies a concentration-based correction to our risk estimates. Details of these baselines are provided in Appendix G.3.

Conservatism and sensitivity to δ\delta. Figure 6 compares empirical risk satisfaction across different failure levels δ\delta. UCB-RC and LTT retain very high satisfaction rates (close to 100%100\%) across different δ\delta, including δ=0.4\delta=0.4, for which the requirement is only 1−δ=0.61-\delta=0.6. Although these rates satisfy the nominal requirement, they remain very conservative regardless of how we choose δ\delta. RCL-HP responds more strongly to the nominal level.

To further examine the calibration of the uncertainty corrections, Figure 8 reports the empirical coverage of the risk upper bounds. UCB-RC maintains coverage close to one across the evaluated values of δ\delta, indicating substantial overcoverage, particularly at lower nominal confidence levels. By comparison, the coverage of RCL-HP varies more closely with 1−δ1-\delta. Together with the risk satisfaction results, this provides evidence that the bootstrap correction is more responsive to the confidence level in these experiments.

These differences are consistent with how the methods construct their uncertainty corrections. LTT combines individual risk tests with a family-wise testing procedure, whose conservatism depends on the tests and the multiple-testing rule employed. For UCB-RC, the Hoeffding-style correction includes a multiplicity term involving log⁡(|Λ|/δ)\log(|\Lambda|/\delta) and depends on the effective sample size neff​(λ)=1∑iwi​(λ)2,n_{\mathrm{eff}}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{\sum_{i}w_{i}(\lambda)^{2}}, where the weights are normalized to sum to one. More concentrated weights reduce this effective sample size and increase the correction uncertainty and upper bounds. Together, weight concentration and the multiplicity adjustment can produce conservative upper bounds. RCL-HP instead calibrates the maximum fluctuation jointly over the candidate family using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap, accounting for dependence among the candidate-wise risk estimates.

Robustness to distribution shift. Conservative uncertainty correction does not by itself ensure robustness or risk satisfaction under distribution shift. In particular, the original i.i.d. guarantee of LTT does not directly apply to our settings.

Figure 7 compares LTT and RCL-HP on SafetyBench with warm-up sizes m0∈{512,1024,4096}m_{0}\in\{512,1024,4096\}, where warm-up observations are collected under the initial policy before online calibration begins. For m0=512m_{0}=512 and 10241024, LTT maintains the risk below the target and empirical risk satisfaction above the nominal level throughout the evaluated trajectory. For m0=4096m_{0}=4096, however, LTT exhibits violations in later rounds: the risk exceeds the target, and empirical risk satisfaction falls below the nominal level. RCL-HP maintains the risk below the target and empirical satisfaction above the nominal level at every evaluated round across all three settings.

This pattern is consistent with a mismatch between the historical calibration distribution and the current policy. At a given online round, a larger m0m_{0} increases the fraction of calibration observations collected under the initial policy. When subsequent policies induce different distributions, evaluating current-policy risk using the historical observations, collected by the initial policy, without adjusting for this mismatch can lead to unreliable risk estimates. The results illustrate that the LTT baseline can fail to maintain the nominal risk satisfaction level in this setting, despite its conservative behavior.

G.6 Experiments to Validate Assumptions and Lemmas in Theorem 4.5

G.6.1 Approximation Error

Dataset and evaluation.

We use the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset, containing 569 observations and 30 features. Malignant cases are treated as the positive class, and the evaluated risk is the false-negative rate (FNR). The sample sizes below refer to the observations used to construct the permutation weights, rather than the entire dataset. We distinguish two sources of approximation error: fixing the learned policy sequence under permutation and replacing exact permutation marginals with estimation from the Sinkhorn algorithm. Let padp^{\mathrm{ad}} denote the exact adaptive weights, pfrp^{\mathrm{fr}} the exact weights for the frozen policy sequence, and qq the computed Sinkhorn weights. We compare normalized weight vectors using total variation, TV⁡(u,v)=12​∑i|ui−vi|\operatorname{TV}(u,v)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}|u_{i}-v_{i}|.

Exact calculation using fixed policy sequence versus Sinkhorn.

We compare exact permutation marginals with Sinkhorn weights computed from the same frozen policy matrix. The two checkpoints contain 70 and 80 observations. We compute exact weights using grouped permanent dynamic programming.

In Table 3, we see that the TV of the two weights is approximately 0.0010.001, and the reported FNR differences are approximately 0.200.20 and 0.180.18 percentage points with only 7%7\% gap. These results indicate small relaxation errors for the evaluated frozen policy sequence. We believe that this gap will be even smaller with a larger dataset.

Adaptive exact weights versus Sinkhorn.

We run experiments across five data collection rounds, with 10 data points per round. The exact adaptive weights account for policy updates under alternative observation orderings, rather than fixing the observed policy sequence. This comparison therefore includes both policy-freezing and Sinkhorn-relaxation errors. We show the results in Table 4. The total variation is 0.00132.

G.6.3 Assumption of the Log Range Not Increasing

For a positive weight vector or matrix pp, define the log range of the row as: Δ⁡(p)=maxi⁡log⁡pi−mini⁡log⁡pi\Delta(p)=\max_{i}\log p_{i}-\min_{i}\log p_{i}. We test whether the assumption that the Sinkhorn weight row QQ has a smaller log range than the original policy matrix JJ holds in practice, leading to smaller worst-case variance than IPS.

Intuitively, the bounded log-range assumption means that after permutation, the weight is not too "sharp" and is smoother. We interpret this as minimizing KL while maximizing entropy. We directly evaluated the log-range of the permutation weights of the policy selected at every round. Δ​J\Delta J and Δ​Q\Delta Q are the log-range values before and after the Sinkhorn approximation. Table 5 shows the satisfaction rate, i.e., Δ​Q<Δ​J\Delta Q<\Delta J is 97%97\%, indicating that the assumption holds in most cases. We also see that the average log range of the permutation weight is much smaller than that of the original policy.

G.6.4 Empirical Evaluation of the Assumption in Theory

We first evaluate whether the variance of the bootstrap estimator asymptotically converges to the variance of the true error using the breast cancer dataset. We also evaluate the Lemma derived directly from the assumption to show the validity of our assumptions.

Variance Matching

We evaluate variance matching for our Sinkhorn-based Gaussian bootstrap using the breast cancer dataset.

We sample 100 data points with replacement at each step until we have 2,500 data points for calibration and estimate the risk. We estimate the variance of the risk estimate with respect to the true risk by repeating the experiments 500 times. We also run 500 seeds, report the variance from bootstrapping each run, and compare it with the ground-truth variance. We report the results with the ratio VarEstimatedVarGT\frac{\text{Var}_{\text{Estimated}}}{\text{Var}_{\text{GT}}} in the Figure 9.

As the number of data points increases, the variance ratio approaches 1, indicating that the variances match.

The centering term di,jd_{i,j} is evaluated exactly over all context-action pairs, ensuring 𝔼⁡[ψi,j∣ℱi−1]=0\mathbb{E}[\psi_{i,j}\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=0.

For the test point, we set 𝝍t+1=𝟎\bm{\psi}_{t+1}=\bm{0}. Its estimated contribution is retained in the sum, using the corresponding Sinkhorn weight and the assigned worst-case loss Lt+1=1L_{t+1}=1.

The experimental results are shown in Figure 10(c). We observe that the mean squared discrepancy between the estimated and true first-order contributions decreases. This provides empirical support for Lemma F.11.

G.7 Implementation Details

We conduct experiments on one A5000 GPU for Breast Cancer and Stock Investment. One seed experiment takes  2-5 minutes. We use RTX PRO 6000 for SafetyBench. Fine-tuning takes  20 minutes, and the calibration process takes 1.5 hours. MedicalQA doesn’t involve any GPU usage and takes  3 minute.

Broader Impact

Our work aims to ensure the safe deployment of online policy learning algorithms, which is crucial for reliable online and sequential decision-making. Providing principled risk-control guarantees during learning and deployment is essential to make online policy learning more trustworthy and practically usable. However, high-probability guarantees are asymptotic and depend on the stated assumptions and a sufficiently large dataset; they should not be interpreted as unconditional finite-sample safety guarantees. If these assumptions fail or estimation errors are underestimated, a deployed policy may exceed the target risk.
